📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

Industry observers note that A grizzly cub, massive as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

“Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, big and fast and flat to the ground.

I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Excerpted from the novel Nearshore (Viking, 2026).

Palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

He’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

Recent findings suggest that the wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while. It looked to be stirring up some kind of suicidal whirlpool.

It Would’ve Been the Best Duck Hunt of Our Lives. Instead, We Almost Died

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the greatest ordeals of my life began on a bleak, heavily overcast day, with a strong north wind and temperatures never rising above 22°.
  • It has been revealed that the Floodway was still timberland.
  • Sources indicate that george was an able physician and loyal friend, but he could never become a hunter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the greatest ordeals of my life began on a bleak, heavily overcast day, with a strong north wind and temperatures never rising above 22°. Dr. George Dahnke and I, both of Memphis, had decided to hunt ducks in the Floodway over in Arkansas. We’d heard reports that mallards were swarming on Section 16 of the Floodway, and the ducks were there, as we were to learn the hard way.

It has been revealed that the Floodway was still timberland. About 100,000 acres of it had been dammed and canalized to prevent the St. Francis River from flooding the towns of Marked Tree and Parkin. The forest floor was flooded all year, hence, the lure for ducks.

Sources indicate that george was an able physician and loyal friend, but he could never become a hunter. Though he was an enthusiast who tried hard, he began hunting too late in life and was too dedicated to the practice of medicine to give much thought to hunting. Further, he was not physically fit, being too soft through lack of exercise.

Sources indicate that we drove to the Floodway with my father-in-law, Mr. Ambrose, who was past 70 years of age. He realized that he was not up to the effort involved in as much boating as George and I planned to do, so he arranged for a local guide to paddle his boat and keep him close to the clubhouse.

This story, “I’ll Never Hunt Ducks Again,” appeared in the March 1982 issue of Outdoor Life.

In a recent development, george and I pushed off before daylight and began motoring with the current down the main ditch, No. 62, which flowed south. By dawn we’d gone about half the eight miles we intended to go. Long before we reached our goal we had seen enough flushing mallards to be reasonably sure of plenty of action. Finally we left the main ditch, No. 62, shut down the little outboard engine, and prepared to paddle west through the woods. The ducks continued to work overhead, seemingly intent on reaching the area we had chosen.

According to recent reports, we found an ideal situation, where thick bunch brush, covered by a dense network of vines, overlooked half an acre of open water. We pushed the boat under that natural blind and broke out ports in the tangle so that we could fire from the boat. I threw six decoys into the shallow water, and the setup appeared to be ideal. The only problem was my apprehension that our limits would come too easily and rapidly for the keenest sport.

The ducks flew high overhead in a constant stream but paid no attention to the invitations sounded on my Turpin call. I did my utmost to make every quack, chatter or chuckle perfect, but all the birds were homing in on one small area. Obviously, some other hunters had a better setup than we did.

It has been revealed that “George, those fellows are the lousiest callers I’ve ever heard,” I said. “But they’re getting the ducks. Those fellows doing that tooting are champs for luck!”.

It has been revealed that related: Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure.

George blinked, then said, “J.D., I hadn’t thought about it, but we can hear those jokers calling, and they’re no good.”.

Sources indicate that “Yeah! And getting all the ducks!” I said, thoroughly disgusted. “Watch that bunch. They set their wings and are gliding straight in without circling.”.

It has been revealed that I was envious, as well as curious. In all my years of duck hunting I had never encountered a similar situation.

“Those guys sound like hogs feeding and hounds running,” George noted. “And geese honking, and cows lowing!” I added.

Suddenly I realized why the masses of ducks were heedless. “George,” I said. “Those are ducks doing the calling! We have been sitting here like fools, criticizing the techniques of real ducks! What a dummy I am!”.

“How do you know they’re real ducks?” George asked.

“How many shots have you heard?” I noted. “If there were hunters over there, we would have heard them shooting.”.

Say, you’re right!” George remarked.

“You stay here.” I suggested. “I’ll wade over and put that raft of ducks up. We can’t do any good as long as we have to compete with real ducks on the water.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that beaten, bruised, and a bit smarter than it was on opening day, the old buck slowly moves from his bed. The sun just set, but he’s not anywhere close to a substantial field yet.

Keeping it in low gear, the deer alternates between taking a couple steps and scanning its surroundings. On pins and pine needles, the buck nears the edge of the bedding area, hits a smaller trail other deer rarely use, and sets course for the distant standing soybean field.

Sources indicate that sitting high in a tall cedar tree, you wait for any sign of the massive 10-pointer you’ve been after all season. Any moment now….

It has been revealed that suddenly, you see the front legs of a deer standing in the timber on the hill above. Seconds turn into minutes, and the deer doesn’t move. Finally, it covers a few more yards, and that massive 10-point rack comes into view. Only 50 yards separate the late-season hunter and the buck — all because he focused on patterning a late-season buck. Here’s how to do it.

Some elements of patterning a late-season deer take place before the hunt. It’s a good time to reassess the situation, reflect on the past, and take a new approach.

Hunt new spots. Late-season deer are especially wary. At this point in the season, some deer have been shot and shot at. Virtually all deer have felt pressure, so it’s crucial to spend some time scouting areas that weren’t hunted previously. Oftentimes, it’s these places deer slink into during the late season. Even if these spots seem less than perfect, it’s worth scouting them.

Industry observers note that reflect on the Past: Consider past seasons and how deer behaved then. Refer to trail camera intel and sightings of deer in the field. Digging into the details of past seasons will help you understand current and future deer movement. If conditions and habitat factors and food sources line up similarly to how they have in the past, deer should exhibit similar patterns. This takes a lot of the guesswork out of game planning.

Effective deer hunting is all about knowing whitetail lines of movement. Studying the lines that take whitetails from point A to point B is crucial for selecting a high-odds stand or blind location.

Locate the food. Food drives late-season deer behavior. Locate the food, and you find the deer. That noted, deer place emphasis on the limiting resource factor. If safe bedding cover is scarce, they’ll find what’s available and travel farther to reach food. If safe bedding cover is abundant, they’ll bed closer to the available food.

Sources indicate that hunt a late-season kill plot. It’s too late to plant now, but if you planted a late-season food plot, it’s time to cash in. Standing corn, standing soybeans, winter wheat, turnips, and much more, make excellent late-season food sources for whitetails. Placing a winter food plot in a strategic location, such as near solar or thermal bedding cover, is a solid play. It can make the patterning process much easier.

Recent findings suggest that save a food plot. As fall gives way to winter, and food sources wane, deer hammer what’s left. The only way to keep a food plot viable into the late season is to prevent deer and other critters from consuming it earlier. That requires planting the right plant species (like brassicas), keeping deer out (with an electric exclusion fence), and opening it up at just the right time. Thus, you’re saving a food plot for the final days of the season.

Find the thermal bedding. Deer use certain types of bedding cover to combat the winter cold. The most common is thermal bedding (especially in flatter areas without much topography). This comes in the form of cedars, spruce, and pine trees. These evergreens shield deer from the rain, sleet, and snow. Furthermore, these thick plants block bitter-cold winds. Equally impressive is that the air temperature is several degrees warmer amidst the conifers.

Industry observers note that identify south-facing slopes. Deer also benefit significantly from the sun. Because the winter sun rises in the southeast, and sets in the southwest, the southerly face of the slope will be warmer on sunny days. So long as deer aren’t pressured there, it should be the primary deer bedding spot for the general area.

In a recent development, glass from afar. Even in today’s world of cellular trail cameras, the age-old tactic of sitting down and raising the glasses is still a good one. You’ll need open country like fields that serve as primary food sources.

It has been revealed that watch a buck’s route. To pattern a deer is to know its general whereabouts and habits. These include bedding areas, food sources, water sources, staging areas, and the travel routes in between. By watching a buck’s route in person, scouting for tracks, or monitoring via trail cameras, hunters can watch a buck’s route and make firm prepares after identifying the target.

Recent findings suggest that reposition trail cameras. While in the field scouting for deer sign, positioning stands, filling feeders, and completing other tasks, go ahead and set up some new trail camera locations. Where legal, focus on the cellular variety. If cameras that were productive early season have gone dead now, don’t be afraid to move them to more promising spots.

After determining your target buck’s lines of movement, it’s time to make a move. Put the proposal in motion, or call an audible as needed.

In a recent development, still hunt the edges. While still hunting works best during the rut when deer are more distracted, it can be effective during the late season, too. If you’ve had trouble patterning a late-season buck, consider still hunting. Moving slowly, yet covering ground, might help piece together remaining clues to hunt a deer you know about, or help find a fresh one altogether. Still hunting is especially effective for morning hunts, when it’s often difficult to hike straight into a stand location without spooking deer.

Track down your buck. A fresh blanket of snow makes for prime tracking conditions, and if you have an idea about a buck’s travel lines, tracking becomes a lot easier. Go slow, and keep your eyes peeled. Chances are good he’ll see you first, but move slowly enough, and you’ll have a chance at a shot.

According to recent reports, be mobile and flexible. Whether you are hunting from a treestand, hunting blind, or still hunting through cover, remember to be flexible. Be patient and execute your plan, but don’t be so attached that it stays in motion even after it becomes clear another tactic is better. Remember that each deer hunt is its own unique experience. Thus, hunters should always implement tactics based on the situation.

Late-season deer hunting is no cakewalk. Deer are skittish and the bitter cold can be tough to endure. Nonetheless, hunt hard, and you just might bag a buck. Focus on new, unpressured spots, protected bedding areas, and primary food sources to finally punch that buck tag.

We Forgot the Thanksgiving Turkey. So We Went Striper Fishing Instead

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Striped Turkey,” appeared in the November 1955 matter of Outdoor Life.
  • Industry observers note that five minutes after the arrival of my Boston brother and his family at my home in East Hampton, Connecticut, we discovered a calamity.
  • We thought they were to bring it, and they thought we were to get it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Striped Turkey,” appeared in the November 1955 matter of Outdoor Life.

Industry observers note that five minutes after the arrival of my Boston brother and his family at my home in East Hampton, Connecticut, we discovered a calamity. Neither of us had bought a turkey, and it was already 10 o’clock Thanksgiving Eve.

We thought they were to bring it, and they thought we were to get it.

Above the hysterical babble, I made a daring suggestion: “Maybe we can make do with something else.”.

“Nonsense,” my wife snorted. “What would you like? Cranberry sauce, mashed potatoes, pumpkin pie, and beans?”.

Brother Don raised a hand commanding silence.

Sources indicate that “This is probably the best thing that could have happened,” he said. “Be a good lesson for the kids. Teach them to be resourceful. Now I have a plan. . . .”.

Recent findings suggest that “That’s crazy,” I interrupted as I saw his eyes fixed on my old single-shot .22 standing in the corner. “There hasn’t been a turkey shot in Connecticut for 200 years.”.

“I wasn’t planning to hunt. You and I were figuring on fishing in the morning, right?” he asked.

“O.K.,” he said, “it’s simple, instead of fishing just for sport, we fish to eat.”.

“That’s out!” both wives screamed.

In a recent development, “For weeks the children have been learning about Thanksgiving in school,” Cynthia informed us. “They’ve drawn pictures of turkeys, talked about turkeys, and written poems about turkeys. And it just won’t be Thanksgiving without a turkey.”.

“That’s silly,” I replied. “If you figure that way, then we’ve got to find some Indians, too.”.

“Sure,” Don added. “That bird guff is just propaganda cooked up by the turkey growers.”.

“I’ll bet, if the truth were known, the pilgrims ate striped bass instead of turkey,” I remarked.

Industry observers note that “Of course they did,” Don noted. He rubbed his hands in satisfaction. “It’s all settled now. You girls sleep late in the morning and leave everything to us. We’ll be back by noon with a striper.”.

“We’ll get some scallops while we’re at it, too,” I promised.

“Even some oysters,” Don injected.

Sources indicate that the kids were snake dancing from room to room and shouting a song about gobble, gobble, gobblers as they went. The wives stood around, looking incredulous, so Don felt it necessary to add a clincher. When I got the drift of what he was proposing I gave him a kick, but it was too late. He promised that if we weren’t back by 1 o’clock — with the fish — we’d all go out to a fine restaurant for dinner.

When we were alone I told him, “You didn’t have to promise that. The bill for this mob will sink us.”.

“Nonsense. Have some confidence. We’ll catch fish,” he countered.

According to recent reports, it was still dark when we left the house next morning, and you could smell the cold — just before your nostrils were pinched shut. While the car engine warmed up, I dashed back into the house, made some instant coffee, and poured it into a vacuum bottle. I must have awakened my sleeping wife.

“Take your time,” she called from upstairs. “We’ll be dressed and ready to go at 1 o’clock.”.

Industry observers note that in addition to our tackle, we stuck a long-handled scallop net into the car. Neither Don nor I mentioned much as we drove the 25 miles to Niantic, where I keep my boat. He kept fiddling with the radio, tuning in each station’s weather report, no doubt figuring that eventually he’d hear a report that promised “fair and rapidly rising temperatures.”.

I mulled over our chances for getting fish and the subject of frostbite striper fishing in general. Most of the bass caught in Connecticut are the small, school fish. During the warmer months these 2 to 10-pounders look like mighty small potatoes, compared to the 40 and 50-pounders taken in other coastal states. We get our compensation in the winter, when the giant bass of neighboring states have taken off for warmer climes. Our stripers stay with us. They’re natives and provide fishing in even the coldest weather. It’s surprising how large a 10-pound fish looks in the month of January.

When we arrived at the dock it was still dark, but my boat gleamed ghostlike in a heavy shroud of frost. Ice lay thick in the bottom.

Hot spot for this refrigerated striper angling is in the southeast corner of the state, in the Thames and Niantic rivers. In the past I got action almost 50 percent of the time. That is, every second trip I stood a good chance of taking fish. Unfortunately, that reckoning doomed this Thanksgiving-Day trip from the start, for I’d done very well the last time out. But then, who wants to quit when they’re ahead?

Industry observers note that when we arrived at the dock it was still dark, but my boat gleamed ghostlike in a heavy shroud of frost. Ice lay thick in the bottom. I realized my boating season was about over. I’d have to haul it out within a few days, for the intermittent thaws and freezes hurt a boat. And anyway, most winter bass fishing is done from shore.

According to recent reports, instead of using a bailing can, Don chipped away on the ice with a screwdriver, while I attached the motor to the stern and loaded our gear. By the time we were under way, the sun had begun to light up the undersides of long, stringy clouds.

“Where shall we start operations?” I asked.

“Play the hunches,” Don suggested. “What goes with Thanksgiving?”.

“O.K.,” I said, and swung the boat in the direction of Turkey Point, the most popular spot on the Niantic River. At that early hour we would have the place to ourselves. Speeding along, our boat left the slightly rippled surface of the channel and entered an area that looked somewhat like an oil slick.

It was ice — a microscopically thin glaze of the stuff.

“This will cut our lines,” he warned.

I told him I didn’t think so. “It’s so thin, and it doesn’t seem to be around the point.”.

Industry observers note that A stronger current there had evidently prevented the ice formation. I killed the motor and we started casting to the deep water that lay along the edge of a submerged sandbar.

It has been revealed that there are two popular and proven techniques used in the Niantic for stripers. One is to troll sand or bloodworms behind spinner blades, and the other is casting (usually with spinning tackle) white, weighted bucktails. These are often used with a trailing pork strip. We had worms, lures and tackle to exploit either system.

It was still bitter cold and the sun hadn’t made much progress harvesting our crop of frost. We cast with extra vigor to get warm.

Recent findings suggest that several other boats raced up the river, as though in fear we were cleaning out the fish. One boat eased up to within 50 feet of us, put out a trolling line, and before the worm was decently moist, had hooked a fish.

In a recent development, “How do you like that!” Don moaned as we watched a five-pounder swung aboard. “We’ve been here for an hour and haven’t even had a strike.”.

Industry observers note that “Maybe it’s going to take trolling to score this morning,” I noted. I brought my bucktail in and prepared to fix a trolling rig.

I glanced up and saw that another fellow in a different boat with a bowing rod — right where we’d drifted through. We watched his line slicing the water, and finally the flashing silver as he netted his catch.

“It isn’t just the trollers that are getting fish,” Don noted.

Recent findings suggest that I decided to stick with casting. I tried every retrieve I could think of — slow, fast, and in between; with action and without.

It had warmed up enough to shed one layer of clothing. The warmth was welcome, but each passing minute meant we were that much nearer our 1 o’clock deadline.

It has been revealed that “Maybe we’re fishing too fast,” Don said. “Possibly, because so much depends on it, we’re rushing our retrieves.”.

“That’s ridiculous,” I argued. “We’ve been trying everything.”.

According to recent reports, we couldn’t keep our eyes off the other boats. By then there were about a dozen, some trolling, others drifting as their occupants cast. Stripers were being caught by everyone, so it seemed, but us.

Sources indicate that “This is justice,” Don groaned. “Here these guys are fishing for fun. They’ll go home, dump their fish into an icebox, mix a Martini, then sit down to a turkey dinner, while we . . .” he shrugged hopelessly.

Industry observers note that “It doesn’t make sense,” I added. “We’re using the same lures, fishing the same water, and as fishermen we’re at least as good as they are.”.

It has been revealed that “Don’t place any bets on that,” Don kidded. “Let’s try trolling.”.

In a recent development, we rigged up one line to go deep and the other to work shallow. I regulated the speed of the boat so the long sandworms trailed enticingly. Then, remembering a trip when a different technique had paid off, I rigged an extra outfit and stuck a shapeless gob of worms on that hook.

Time was passing; it was after 9:30 when we started trolling. We headed upriver. An acquaintance of mine was trolling downriver, and we killed motors to exchange confidences.

Recent findings suggest that “Pretty good,” I answered. “How’re you doing?”.

According to recent reports, “Pretty good. Got three or four — sort of slowing up now, though. Guess early in the morning is best.” My friend started his motor and waved farewell.

Don was fit to be tied. “Imagine that,” he noted. “Three or four fish. Can’t he count? Is he a liar? ‘Sort of slowing up now,’ the man said. Well, anyway, for us things can’t get any slower.” Don disgustedly yanked his rod and started reeling in the line that had sunk to the bottom while we were talking. Suddenly his rod tip started twitching. “Holy cow!” he yelled. “I’ve got a fish.”.

Sources indicate that A second later he shook his head as the line came in too easily. “Guess not. Probably just some weed.”.

He kept reeling and landed the smallest, most ridiculous-looking flatfish I’ve ever seen. He held it up in brief contempt before tossing it back. Lady luck wasn’t just ignoring us, she was giving us the bird.

Sources indicate that all morning we’d noticed two men in a bright-green runabout who were having frequent action. Now, as they trolled by, I saw the chap at the motor slyly drop something over the stern.

“They’re chumming. I bet that’s the answer,” Don remarked. “I’ve seen it done before. Bits of worm are tossed over, the bass pick these up as appetizers, and when the large trolled worm comes by they grab it.”.

“Should we give it a try?” I asked.

Industry observers note that “We haven’t enough worms. Besides, others around here catch fish without chumming.”.

Recent findings suggest that I looked at my watch — 10 o’clock. We’d been fishing almost five hours with nothing to show but Don’s flatfish.

Recent findings suggest that “Do you suppose any of these people would sell a couple —” A tremendous yank on my line shut me up fast. I reached down and snapped the motor into neutral. It stalled and suddenly everything was as quiet as a house without a TV set. Then I thought I heard the taut monofilament sizzling through the water, but it was my own excited breathing.

Recent findings suggest that I knew it was a good fish. I loosened the drag to let it run, and the fish took my line in a wide circle around the boat. We were in the middle of the river and I couldn’t see anything around to cause a snag. All I had to do was keep my head. To be safe, I loosened the drag some more. And then, unbridled, the fish really took off.

“Put some weight on him!” Don yelled.

“Just keep cool and take it easy,” I kept telling myself. Using finger pressure against the spool, I brought the fish to a sluggish stop. I started pumping the rod and it felt as if I were bringing the heavy boat to the fish rather than the fish to the boat.

“It’s a good one.” Don had seen it.

Then I saw it, and it was a beauty. Don had the net deep in the water, and I held my breath as I led the tugging striper to him. With a “wooosh” of the net, the fish was ours. I let my breath go and flopped down on my open tackle box, immune to the pain of an upturned 8/0 hook.

The fish pulled the pointer of my pocket scale below the 12-pound mark — the heaviest striped bass I’ve taken from that river. It was large enough for our requirements, and since time was at a premium, we decided to go after the scallops.

We gunned the boat back to the dock to get one of the 15¢ permits entitling you to one bushel of Niantic scallops. These scallops are considered a delicacy throughout Connecticut. The season opens in October, and by Thanksgiving the beds have been well worked over.

In a recent development, the technique for taking these shellfish is basically simple — one merely uses the long-handled net as a scoop over the bottom. Luck and skill determine the percentage of scallops in a net full of mud, seaweed, empty shells, and stones.

Luck played on our side for a change, and we came across an area where Don made one productive scoop after another. Within 30 minutes we had all we needed.

“We’re really cooking now,” Don said. “How about the oysters?”.

Industry observers note that I looked at my watch. “Suits me. The tide will be just about right.”.

Recent findings suggest that the oysters we had in mind were the small, rock variety that are found at low tide along stony beaches. We decided on a place a few miles down the coast, where we usually had good luck before. We moored the boat, got our gear, fish, and scallops into the car, and were on our way.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m starving,” Don noted. “Can we stop for a hamburger?”.

It has been revealed that I shook my head. “Nope, we’re running a tight schedule. It’s 11:30 already.”.

Industry observers note that this beach, like most of the Connecticut shoreline at this season, was deserted, the cottages boarded up. The day, by that time, was warm, and the sun made sand and water glisten with midsummer gaiety. It was a particularly low tide, and when we got to the rocky point we found oysters aplenty.

I was carrying a sack, but it was several minutes before anything went in it. With drawn knives and the appetites of shipwrecked sailors, we fell upon the oysters. Eaten right on the spot, the clean, saline taste is something you don’t ever get enough of. Oysters disappeared as fast as popcorn at a western movie.

We finally snapped out of this orgy and gathered stuffing for our bag.

We arrived home with five minutes to spare and everyone went to work. The women got busy in the kitchen, while Don and I opened oysters. The older kids readied the scallops. Soon the perfume of baking bass hinted at what was to come. By this time, the kids had forgotten all about turkeys.

Our first course was oysters on the half shell, followed by generous helpings of scallops, broiled in butter. Then came the bass — baked a delicate brown on the outside, fat with chestnut stuffing inside. It’s true there were no drumsticks to fight over, but on the other hand, there was no neck or tail.

Afterward, Don lay back on a couch and — after giving a gentle pat to his mid-section — noted, “You know, this dinner was terrific, but next year we can improve on it.”.

“We’ll take the kids along, and while you and I are out snagging striped turkey, they can dig clams for a chowder.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Winter bivy sacks were first developed as solo shelters for mountaineering and climbing where participants were interested in lightweight and highly compressible camping gear. Bivy Sacks are also an attractive option for backpacking hunters, backcountry skiers, and winter backpackers who want the lightest and smallest shelter they can carry for overnight or emergency use.

Recent findings suggest that winter bivy sacks are different from three-season bivy sacks, which are often used in conjunction with a tarp for insect and splashback protection, where rain hitting the ground can bounce back and wet your quilt or sleeping bag. In contrast, a winter bivy sack is intended as a standalone shelter or used with a snow shelter such as a trench or snow cave. Winter bivy sacks tend to be much higher in volume to hold winter-weight sleeping bags without compressing the insulation and work best in dry and cold conditions where precipitation is in the form of snow.

It has been revealed that the biggest advantage of a winter bivy sack is that you can use it anywhere you want to stop and sleep. Most models don’t require tent stakes or poles, and they pack down very small, which is great when you want to keep your winter gear lightweight and compact. Most winter bivy sacks use waterproof/breathable top fabrics to reduce internal condensation and waterproof base fabrics to keep your sleeping bag and pad dry. Insect netting is also available in some cold weather bivy sacks and can be useful when they’re used in spring conditions when bugs begin to emerge,.

According to recent reports, there are many advantages to sleeping in a waterproof bivy sack over a tent. It is easy to find a place to put a bivy sack at night since it only requires as much space as your sleeping pad and sleeping bag. Simply unroll your bivy sack, slip your sleeping pad and sleeping bag inside, and crawl in. This makes them suitable for sleeping on narrow mountain ledges or in forested glades where there’s just enough space to lie between two trees.

There are no tent stakes to freeze into the ground so you can get inside without delay and get warm. Being waterproof, you don’t have to lie on top of a groundsheet either, since the bottom of a waterproof bivy sack is designed to keep you dry. Bivy sacks also add a few degrees of insulation to your sleep system and make great emergency shelters for solo winter hikers, provided you carry a sleeping pad and enough insulation to get through the night.

Bivy sacks are much more confining than tents, with only enough space for you and a few small personal items. You can’t really do anything inside one except listen to podcasts or go to sleep. It’s awkward to change out of your wet clothes or put on dry clothes inside, depending on the type of bivy sack you have; it can be damn hard to put on your boots, even to go for a pee at night. There’s no place to store your backpack, and the rest of your gear will be fully exposed at night without any cover.

Bivy sacks are also more prone to internal condensation than a tent, even when manufactured with waterproof breathable materials. You’re best off keeping them open or unzipped at night to reduce the temperature difference between the inside of the bivy and the outside, which causes condensation. Tent condensation occurs for the same reason, but tents have better ventilation and more volume, so it’s easier to keep your sleeping bag dry when it occurs.

Despite these disadvantages, I have friends who swear by their winter bivy sacks because they’re so fast to deploy compared to a tent or tarp. I’ve used winter bivy sacks and can appreciate their strengths, but winter nights last a very long time, and it’s nice to have a little extra space to change your clothes or sleep with your gear inside your tent. Whichever you choose depends on what you’re trying to accomplish.

There are three types of winter bivy sacks to choose from:.

Sources indicate that there are two types of hooped bivy sacks: those with front entrances that you slide into feet first and those that you can enter from the side. Both come with one more short fiberglass or carbon fiber rods that give shape to the hood and prevent it from collapsing onto your head or torso.

The head-end of a hooped front entrance bivy is usually screened with a solid cover that can be zippered closed for warmth or to block wind or rain. This design provides good ventilation for your head and helps to expel the water vapor in your breath. The Outdoor Research Helium UL Bivy is a good example of the front entry hooped design.

Recent findings suggest that side-entry hooped bivy sacks usually have a zipper along one side so you can easily get in and out of them. This design is also easier to vent because you can roll up the top cover in dry weather to reduce internal condensation. The Outdoor Research Alpine XT Bivy is a good example of a hooped bivy with a side entrance.

The simplest and lightest-weight winter bivy sacks are little more than sleeping bag covers. Some have drawstrings that you can pull closed over your head; some have shaped mummy-style hoods or simple slits above the face for ventilation. While not as livable or as well-ventilated as the hooped bivy sack designs described above, they do the job if you want a highly compressible, ultralight weather protection for your sleep system.

There are multiple features and trade-offs to consider when choosing a winter bivy sack.

A waterproof/breathable top fabric is important for venting water vapor and reducing internal condensation that can make your sleeping bag wet. However, unlike rain jackets, most bivy sack manufacturers do not list the laboratory measurements used to rate waterproofing (hydrostatic head, abbreviated “HH”) or breathability (movable water transmission rate, abbreviated “MVTR”). That can make performance comparisons between different bivy sacks difficult.

In a recent development, if headroom matters, consider a bivy shelter with a hooped design. These bivy sacks come with a flexible pole that slides into the hood to create more volume around your face and shoulders. The tradeoff is that they tend to be heavier than more minimal bivy sacks.

Sources indicate that winter bivy sacks tend to be high volume to fit bulky winter sleeping bags and inflatable pads with a high R-value. When choosing a bivy sack you want to ensure that there is enough room for your sleeping bag insulation to fully loft and that it’s not compressed by having too tight a fit.

It has been revealed that it’s much easier to get in and out of a bivy sack that has a zipper along the side than one that only has a “hatch” at the head end, to crawl in and out of. You’ll stay drier if the ground is covered in snow and it’s much easier to put on and take off your shoes.

If you blueprint to bivy in early spring when biting insects emerge, make sure to get a winter bivy sack with a mesh panel over the face so you can sleep without insects biting your face at night. If you only plan to sleep in a bivy sack in winter or in snow caves, a mesh panel will be less notable. For warmer weather use, I’d encourage you to invest in an ultralight bivy sack or bug shelter rather than a winter bivy sack, since they’re much cooler to use. See our 10 Best Backpacking Bug Shelters for our recommended three-season bivy sacks.

Don’t forget to consider the weight of the bivy sack and its packed size, since one of the chief benefits of using a bivy sack is gear weight and size reduction. There’s often a tradeoff between features and weight/size, but some winter bivy sacks are surprisingly lightweight and compressible.

Sources indicate that when in doubt, order a bivy sack (check the retailer’s return policy) and lie in it at home to see if it fits. This will probably tell you a lot more about whether it will work for you than comparing the specs of multiple models listed online. Check that you can fit your sleeping pad and sleeping bag inside, and that the footbox is large enough for your feet.

According to recent reports, there is a class of emergency bivy sacks that are only intended for emergency use such as the SOL Escape Lite Bivy. These are made with thin reflective aluminized fabric and lack the durability or breathability of the multiuse bivy sacks listed above.

#159553. Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2696 w)
📖 Baca

Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer.
  • I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.
  • It has been revealed that hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer. “Look at all the tracks you’ll see with snow covering the ground,” they chorus.

I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.

It has been revealed that hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are. And tracks may not necessarily indicate where deer are likely to be again. One deer can make a lot of tracks.

But if you know how snowfall changes a whitetail’s daily routine, you are starting to understand where you will find tracks — and the deer that made them.

Let’s rehearse some basic facts.

Sources indicate that first, snow normally comes late in most states’ deer seasons. That means whitetails already have been harassed by other hunters. Unless you hunt private land, all deer you are likely to encounter may be wary, even downright spooky. They are moving little during daylight hours. Rutting bucks are probably limiting much of their roaming to the darkness of night.

Second, snowstorms — and most other storms — are accompanied by periods of intensely low barometric pressure. Whitetails tend to roam wide in search of food prior to a storm. But they hole up when snow actually starts to fall. And they stay holed up until the storm passes or at least until it eases off.

Sources indicate that third, while snow means hunters can see deer moving much more easily, it also works the other way around. Deer see the hunter coming a lot farther off. The fact that snow silences the woods forces deer to use their eyes more. Ever spend an hour or two watching a band of deer bedded down after a snowstorm? Their heads are lifted much more often to eyeball the surrounding terrain. Eyes must assume a vigil which ears can no longer accomplish and must provide the essential early warning. Incidentally, your own hearing abilities aren’t helped by snowfall, either. Deer that rustled the crisp frozen leaves of a frosty fall morning won’t be heard walking through a soft cover of new-fallen snow.

Sources indicate that fourth, snow changes whitetail eating habits — particularly heavy snowfall. Meadow grasses may not be pawed at again until spring. Buds, twigs and surviving leafy vegetation take its place. These plants are less nutritious for deer but they are easier to obtain. Waste grains in fields blown clear of snow may promote a concentration of feeding whitetails.

So now you are thinking that snowfall might not be such a boon to hunting?

Actually, it is — if you know how to use it to your advantage.

Whitetails, like all wildlife, are creatures of habit. You can predict a deer’s general reaction to things that impact on its environment. Maybe your predictions won’t be precise but they can be close enough to cut down on the number of fruitless hunting efforts you make.

Pay attention to the weatherman. Be sure you are out hunting on the day before a storm is forecast to arrive. Through changes in barometric pressure, deer sense the oncoming storm. They often move out to feed as heavily as possible — even in the middle of the day — forgoing the usual bedding hours in their hasty urge to stock up before the storm. So be sure to hunt all day.

Pre-storm is the time to concentrate on checking food sources for whitetails. Hunting pressure earlier in the season may have forced the animals to visit open grainfields only at night. If hunter numbers have dwindled — as they do in most states after the first four or five days of the season — start checking those fields again at dawn and dusk. The urge to fill up before a storm may have deer less cautious.

According to recent reports, in woodland areas, check hidden openings or meadow edges where wild herbaceous cover remains. Don’t overlook timber cuttings where saplings provide cover and the lack of an overstory promotes the undergrowth that deer savor. Try the creek bottoms where frost may not have killed the green grasses yet.

It has been revealed that in farmlands, glass the local hay fields or even vegetable patches where potatoes, sugar beets, carrots, turnips or other root-type plants have not all been harvested yet. And visit abandoned orchards where fallen fruit may provide an attraction.

According to recent reports, more than once in a late deer season afternoon, while driving the back roads of farm country near where I live, I have become aware of more and more deer suddenly appearing where few were before. The back edge of a cutover hay field will hold five or six deer, all feeding near a heavy hickory and oak woodlot. Harvested cornfields may have a few animals wandering along, plucking up the waste dumped by corn pickers before it can be plowed under.

Does tend to move farther from cover than bucks, particularly when feeding in daylight hours prior to a storm. But expect surprises. Once, while walking across a partially harvested cornfield to reach a gun blind in the woodlot beyond, I stumbled across a fine eight-point buck. This lone deer, feeding in a 12-row patch of standing corn, was fully 80 yards from the nearest heavy cover. He evidently felt safe among the withered cornstalks. And their rattling in the wind had probably masked the sound of my approach.

Industry observers note that I was so startled, in fact, that I never got off a shot from the slug-loaded 12-gauge that I was carrying. The buck wheeled and bounded away before I could shoot.

According to recent reports, don’t be caught unprepared. You never know where a deer will suddenly appear. I’ve had does dart from brushy drainage ditches — deep ones that were mostly dry or had the damp patches frozen solid by late fall’s icy weather. Ditches provide perfect cover routes to reach open stretches with food. Shelterbelts do so, too.

Industry observers note that once a storm of some magnitude starts, deer simply disappear. Whitetails of both sexes will head for the thickest most protective cover around. Conifers are ideal (pine plantations or cedar swamps in the North Country). In farmlands, overgrown brushy woodlots or thick river bottom or creekbottom cover is an alternative. Here deer will lie down and, unless disturbed by a hunter wandering around in the storm, they will not get up for hours — maybe days.

The hollow hair in deer’s coats provides superb insulation from the snow’s cold and dampness. Curled up into a small oval (judge for yourself how compactly a whitetail can curl up by the sizes of the beds you’ll find a day or so later) deer will ride out the storm, sometimes allowing the snowfall to almost literally cover them. They don’t seek food and they don’t move much — even to stand and stretch.

Because hunters don’t normally slog around in heavy storms, deer are usually undisturbed until the snowfall begins to lessen. If a storm lasts more than a day, deer may move around close to their bedding areas but they won’t venture far.

It is an ideal time, once the storm begins to subside, to mount a deer drive.

Industry observers note that pinpointing whitetail cover won’t be difficult, even with the lack of tracks on new-fallen snow. Just pick the heaviest thickest junk around. Match the size of the cover to the number of drivers and standers you have with you, and you should be able to fill several tags for your group.

Sources indicate that there is a farmland county near my Michigan home which is a mixture of cedar swamp, brushy woodlots and grainfields, plus some pastureland. Every other season or so, myself and about five of my hunting buddies drive over there on a Saturday. At this time, we’ve all just come back from the North Country’s season opener; perhaps half of us have been fortunate enough to have scored on a buck already. The lucky ones drive for their less successful counterparts.

It has been revealed that through the years, we have secured hunting permission by telephone and by long acquaintance with the local landowners, some of whom join us for these drives. Because this area is open to the use of high-power rifles, it takes only about three or four standers to cover all downwind and sidewind exit routes in the cover we visit.

The remainder of us cast back and forth in a line — more or less — of drivers, working silently in the belief that noise startles deer even more than human scent and sends them into headlong flight. We want the whitetails to break cover in a nervous trot, glancing back over their shoulders, not fleeing at top speed.

It has been revealed that because the drivers move and the deer focus their attention on them, the standers get some easy shots. Standers are urged to find natural blinds that will camouflage just a bit of the brilliance of the Blaze Orange garments they wear.

Sources indicate that drivers wear as much Blaze Orange as possible for high visibility. They don’t carry firearms, either, on our drives.

It has been revealed that such minidrives have proved extremely successful. In those years when we all fill tags up north and don’t proposal to visit this county, local landowners call us to see if we’re coming over to help them. It has become a social event. We do go, of course.

Well-conducted drives, frankly, are one of the best ways to kill whitetails all season long — early or late, in snow or without it. If you develop a compatible group of hunters who are all safety conscious, driving may well be the best way to hunt.

It has been revealed that for the single hunter, stillhunting in the snow can prove difficult. The muffling effect snow has on sounds is appealing to stillhunters but they should remember that whitetails bedded in snow can be extremely watchful. That’s true at least while a storm is waning or before the sun reappears with warmth enough to prompt more movement of deer. Whitetails scan their surroundings intently. And because they are not likely to be moving, spotting them will prove that much tougher.

If a stillhunter is extremely patient and slow moving, maybe he has a chance. But the average hunter who enjoys some success stillhunting on bare ground may find snowy days beyond his capability.

Recent findings suggest that there is another factor making things tougher: wind. Snowstorms are often accompanied by high winds, ones that don’t die off when the snow stops falling. Wind makes all wildlife nervous. Their hearing isn’t as useful. Add that problem to the noise-muffling effect snow already has and you come up with doubly watchful whitetails.

According to recent reports, so what about doing what you sometimes hear old-timers describe? Just plant yourself on a big buck’s track and walk him into the ground.

Industry observers note that unless you are a true woodsman, which most of us have neither the time nor the inclination to be, forget it. It sounds rather romantic, as the old sporting books told it, but the method isn’t likely to be very rewarding for the hunter of average skill. Oh, it can be done. And every so often you could be lucky enough to actually walk up on a buck — if you can first figure out which tracks belong to bucks and which belong to does. No, the average lone hunter faced with a snowstorm is better off doing just what the deer do: Wait it out.

Once the storm passes, whitetails will begin to circulate once again. Hunger drives them from their beds but sunny weather after a storm seems to invigorate deer, too. No scientific facts back up this phenomenon and I claim no insight into the psychology of deer. It’s just a gut feeling I have about whitetails based on observations of the ways yearlings almost cavort after a storm passes. Young bucks, not part of the serious breeding process that is probably about over when snow begins to fall, seem to want to spar. They push each other around rather good naturedly. The older does concentrate on finding food. Now’s the time for the smart single hunter to be on his stand or in his blind.

Surprisingly, there’s little need to hurry in the morning, either. Deer must feel the cold to some degree because they seldom stir at the crack of dawn after a very cold night. That fact doesn’t mean a hunter shouldn’t be out before daybreak — as he would be earlier in the season. Some whitetails may be stirring. But many times after a storm I’ve witnessed deer waiting until the sun was shining full upon them, waiting for an hour or more after daylight, before moving out to feed. It’s as if they were lying there, soaking up the warmth of the sun.

As a result, deer will often be feeding — or moving to and from feeding areas — in the middle of the day after the return of good weather conditions. For the man in a blind, deer moving on snow in full daylight are easy to spot.

Industry observers note that remember, also, that bedding areas on southern exposures — places where the effects of the warm sun are felt the most intensely — will be favored by deer. Anytime the temperature is under 35°, deer seem to prefer places where the sun can hit them in the morning. If it is out of prevailing winds, so much the better.

Industry observers note that unlike the majority of Western mule deer, which must move from higher mountain summer range to the valleys each winter, whitetails normally find everything they need to survive in a year-round home. One exception is Michigan’s Upper Peninsula where deer summering in the Lake Superior watershed tend to wander southward toward the more temperate climate of Lake Michigan in late fall and early winter, often before deer season ends. Snowfall prompts even greater movement.

Sources indicate that A few of these whitetails travel quite a distance — 40 or maybe 50 miles. Some don’t move at all but take their chances in the deeper snowfall and reduced winter food conditions of the northern watershed. If you are aware of such a migration where you hunt, take advantage of it. The routes traveled are not always as predictable as the game trails muleys use to move downhill but various general routes are used year after year. Spot blinds accordingly.

It has been revealed that the best advice for winter stand hunting, I think, is to stay put and to stay as comfortable as possible. Dress to remain warm in below-freezing temperatures. Make sure that your blind is well situated and that it is constructed in such a way that it blocks out any stray winds. Get a back rest and sit on a patch of canvas or plastic to keep the snow from soaking through.

I always make sure that I have a Thermos of hot coffee, tea or cocoa handy. A blind means you can move around a little without being seen and a few gulps of warm liquid can brighten a dreary day.

And be patient. Deer won’t move as often or as far in snowy weather — unless it’s a bright warm day with temperatures rising above freezing. If you are hunting alone, be prepared to wait them out. And do it in a place where they’re likely to be: near a food source or along (or in the midst of) the heavier cover where they’re certain to bed down.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

Industry observers note that winter hunting doesn’t have to be a case of survival against the elements. You can be comfortable and successful and see more than just tracks.

This story, “Snowstorm Whitetails,” appeared in the December 1983 problem of Outdoor Life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Backpacking gear has gotten very expensive. But here are 25 backpacking gifts for $25 or less that have a high degree of utility and any backpacker would love to receive.

Recent findings suggest that these handy squeeze bottles were easy to buy when REI sold them, but they’ve been hard to find since. They each hold 1 fluid ounce (29.5 ml) and great for repackaging small quantities of shampoo, conditioner, sunscreen, moisturizer, hand sanitizer, and other cosmetics.

It has been revealed that micro Scissors are super small, super light, and super safe. You’ll find lots of backcountry uses where scissors perform better than a knife and make the job easier. And at just 0.17 oz (4.7 g), they’re definitely worth their weight. The precision-ground stainless steel blades start sharp and stay sharp. The finger holes are oversized and elongated for use with or without thin gloves. A silicone safety cover keeps the sharp tips from stabbing you and your gear. The cover is tethered to the handle, so you’ll never lose it.

Cold Soaking Jars offer a revolutionary way to enjoy your favorite trail meals without the fuss of traditional cooking. Simply add water to your food and let it soak for 30-60 minutes while you hike. No stove, no boiling water, no cleanup. It’s that easy. This leak-proof jar is made of FDA-compliant high-density polyethylene (HDPE) plastic, which is rigid and has good impact and chemical resistance. Its translucent design, smooth inner walls, and ribbed lid make for easy access and cleaning.

According to recent reports, the ultimate in simplicity, this folding pad is your go-anywhere, do-anything comfort companion. Whether you’re taking a trailside break or enjoying a picnic in the park, this pad has your back (and your backside). Lightweight, waterproof, and moisture-resistant, it folds up small and stashes easily in your pack or pocket.

If you’re buying a gift for an Appalachian Trail thru-hiker or section hiker, there’s a pretty good chance that they sleep in trail shelters that have mice. If you want to tickle their funny bone and protect their food bag, give them a set of old-school mouse traps to bring along on their backpacking trips. Just bait them with cheese or peanut butter. I once met an Appalachian thru-hiker named “Stretch” who carried mouse traps from shelter to shelter and would surround his sleeping pad with them each night. Needless to say, I didn’t see many mice in the shelters on that section hike.

It has been revealed that this whistle is one of the most effective emergency signaling devices ever invented. If you need to shout for help, you’ll get very tired, very promptly, using your voice alone. But you can blow a whistle all day long; it is much louder and can be heard above environmental noise like the wind or machinery. This Fox 40 Whistle is so loud it can be heard a mile away.

This 10-pack of ultralight tent platform anchors makes it a snap to set up a tent on a wooden tent site platform. The anchors slide in between the boards and provide a secure anchor to tie down a tent. The highly visible red color also makes them hard to lose.

Reduce the amount of toilet paper used in the backcountry while preventing the dreaded chafing and “monkey butt” that results when your crack isn’t clean. This handy bidet attachment screws onto regular plastic water/soda bottles so you can clean up anywhere, even at the office. Very popular with thru-hikers!

Banish blisters forever with these ingenious Injinji Liner Crew Toe Socks. Wear these light and breathable liner socks under thicker outer socks as a first line of defense against moisture and blisters, or wear them alone as your go-to socks for everyday adventures. Made with Coolmax, these synthetic socks wrap each toe individually, preventing the friction that causes blisters.

In a recent development, chicken Tramper Gear’s Standard Ultralight Wallet uses tough, colorful VX21 Xpac and comes with a water-resistant Uretek zipper to ensure a long life.
