    #159453. A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (930 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).
    • According to recent reports, in 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park.
    • Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).

    According to recent reports, in 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. The 120-foot drop left her paralyzed from the waist down. In a moment, she went from climbing the world’s steepest rock faces to moving in a wheelchair.

    Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks. Some of America’s wildest places were no longer accessible to her.

    “To become disabled, and realize that I can’t even get across the street because there is a curb, for instance, was quite a change in perspective,” she told Climbing‘s sibling publication Outside.

    That’s why Brett founded the accessibility consulting firm Dovetail Trail Consulting to make outdoor spaces more accessible and usable for everyone. With her help, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) debuted a new interactive accessibility map on October 13, connecting visitors with trails, bathrooms, and campsites that are accessible to people with mobility disabilities.

    “People with disabilities don’t want to just go to the one-mile paved trail in the busiest parts of our national parks,” Brett noted.

    Industry observers note that as part of the BLM map, visitors can snap photos of public lands and submit them, along with detailed descriptions of the infrastructure. Other users can then better understand accessibility before they hit the trail.

    In a recent development, “You don’t have to do a construction project,” Brett said. “Just take pictures.”.

    In a recent development, nearly one in 10 Americans have mobility concerns, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For these people, Brett says enjoying the outdoors is not just about finding the right device, but also finding trails that are made for wheels.

    “For a long time we only had one pair of shoes to pick, but now with mobility device technology, we have a whole bunch of types of shoes that we get to choose from, and we want to go use our shoes in a variety of places,” Brett stated.

    Industry observers note that kevin Oliver, chief of the BLM Division for Recreation and Business Services, participated in the three-year map project. He told Outside that the goal is to help people plan their trip and avoid surprises from site conditions.

    “We’re going to continue to work to deliver more information and better information to the recreation public, so that all types of interests can be served,” Oliver told Outside. “The BLM recognizes the work is never really done. You know, we’re always perfecting it.”.

    It has been revealed that the map includes 150 existing accessible recreation opportunities. One such example is McCoy Flats in Utah, a map entry that shows the parking lot’s packed gravel, extended picnic tables, and the entrances to vault toilets.

    According to recent reports, the tool also identifies 74 additional sites where the BLM has proposed improvements. Some, like Colorado’s Blue Valley Ranch Trail, are fully funded and in progress. Others, such as Upcoming Mexico’s Glade Run Adaptive Trail, are still hunting for funding.

    BLM’s new map is one piece of a broader push to expand trail access across federal agencies.

    It has been revealed that gathering the information is only the beginning. Julia Ray, chief operating officer of the adaptability nonprofit Move United, told Outside that keeping information up to date matters just as much.

    Industry observers note that “Trails are kind of living things,” Ray said. “They change with weather and seasons, so it has to be an ongoing process to keep that information current, and where and how that information is shared is still inconsistent.”.

    Move United partnered with Mount Rainier and Grand Canyon National Parks to assess more than 17 miles of trails for accessibility. The organization also created a free trail-access course to help local land managers understand federal accessibility standards.

    Improving access at popular trails is a great way to let more people share in the national park experience, Ray said.

    “If the public go to a trail more than others, that’s probably where anybody else would want to go as well,” she stated. “Everybody deserves the right to access the outdoors, and we are just really excited that there’s some energy around this right now.”.

    Recent findings suggest that for trail customers like Brett, having accessibility details means she can spend less time guessing and more time choosing where to go, what equipment to bring, and how much challenge she wants to take on. Her desire to be in the mountains hasn’t gone away, and as she notes, it never will.

    “I still want to be playing and going to the top of mountains and doing wild and crazy things,” Brett says. “But I also need the information to decide what experience I want.”.

    Sources indicate that she added that including people with disabilities in trail assessment and information gathering can help land managers identify barriers. Some mobility devices can navigate rocks, roots, and steps; a narrow bridge or gate might stop someone instead.

    It has been revealed that “Five miles of the trail might work totally fine, and then there’s a bridge to cross some water, and they just threw down a 12-inch bridge, and after that, there’s five more miles of trail that work just fine,” Brett stated. “But if you’ve never hung out with somebody with a disability, then you might not know what is truly a barrier.”.

    #159452. I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1361 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.
    • That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.
    • It has been revealed that fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The author surfing (Photo: Matthew Berridge).

    “How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.

    That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.

    It has been revealed that fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times. I’m convinced that surfing through cancer treatment saved my sanity, and possibly my life.

    According to recent reports, I grew up about as far from the ocean as you can get, in the Midwest. I moved to Northern California after college and fell in love with the Pacific Ocean. Every time I went to the beach, I was fixated on watching surfers—but never thought I could join them because I was too scared to try. And once I started a family, that dream moved further out of reach.

    Sources indicate that fast-forward to the COVID 2020 pandemic lockdown when the public pool where I swam on a Masters swim team was shut down. I started doing laps in the San Francisco Bay with friends. I’d always been terrified of open water swimming, but after a year of braving the Bay’s chilly, choppy waters every morning, I decided it was time to try surfing. I was already wearing a (three-millimeter triathlon) wetsuit.

    It has been revealed that I was 52, the age when menopause, graying hair, and wrinkles can make women feel invisible. My kids had just left home for college. I needed something significant to fill that hole in my life. I took a surf lesson, and was hooked immediately. On the drive home from the beach, I bought a hooded, five-millimeter wetsuit and booties, and started surfing several mornings a week, collecting phone numbers of women I met in the lineup and parking lot.

    After decades of giving everything I had to everyone around me—work colleagues, kids, husband, dogs, parents, sisters—surfing was just for me.

    Soon I had built a community of women surfers aged 25 to 75 to join me for dawn patrol sessions at our break north of San Francisco and surf trips to Mexico, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, San Diego, and Santa Cruz.

    Sources indicate that surfing made me feel strong and beautiful. So I didn’t want to give that up four years later as I faced down cancer.

    Seeking guidance on how to surf through surgery recovery and treatment, I posted a message on the Facebook “Women Who Surf” group of 39,000: “I just got diagnosed with breast cancer and am looking for other women surfers who surfed through chemo, and surfed after a double mastectomy.”.

    A hundred women weighed in with personal experience of cancer and surfing. Most hadn’t surfed during surgery recovery or chemotherapy due to doctors’ orders, infection risk, weak immune systems, limited mobility, fatigue, and weakness.

    Industry observers note that but one woman told me to go for it: Melanie Ezell, a 42-year-old big wave surfer, based in Oahu, who surfed through ovarian cancer. She became my role model, inspiring me to paddle out as soon as I could.

    According to recent reports, that long-awaited day came after being grounded on land for seven weeks following my double mastectomy. It was three days after my first chemotherapy infusion when my plastic surgeon declared my chest incisions adequately healed. I drove immediately to the beach, paddled out, and felt triumphant when I caught my first wave of the session.

    And I kept paddling out through the remaining 11 rounds of chemotherapy.

    On days when the swell was massive and I was weak with fatigue, I’d claw through the impact zone after riding a wave, leaving my arms drained of power and lungs gasping for air. Once safely outside breaking waves, I’d rest on my board and let sets roll past until my breathing slowed. Still, being in the ocean felt like an antidote to the toxic drugs coursing through my veins. I loved watching the birds and seals, scanning the horizon for incoming sets, paddling into a rising wave, feeling its energy connect with my board.

    Sources indicate that sometimes those sessions lasted only an hour because of my reduced stamina. But they always left me feeling stoked and alive, adjectives easily lost when you spend Tuesday afternoons hooked up to an IV bag pumping the sledgehammer drug Taxol into a port in your chest.

    It has been revealed that after my last chemotherapy session, I started ten rounds of targeted immunotherapy infusions (which I just concluded this month) and began posting GoPro videos on Instagram and Facebook of me surfing bald to inspire other women. I wanted them to see what it looks like when breast cancer takes your breasts and hair, but not your identity.

    Women from around the world reached out to share their own stories: Ellen McLaughlin, a 54-year-old massage therapist and mom surfing through rectal cancer in the chilly waters at the Oregon-California border; 32-year-old Lottie Bakewell from Cornwall, England, surfing through breast cancer and the demands of caring for her one-year-old son and three-year-old daughter; Belen Kimble, a 48-year-old former professional longboarder, World Surf League commentator, surf performance coach, and single mom in New South Wales, Australia, surfing through breast cancer; and Caroline Wilhelm, a 55-year-old surfer and competitor from Los Angeles who took my cue to keep surfing through her breast cancer.

    Backed by growing research showing that physical activity during cancer treatment offsets chemotherapy side effects and improves recovery and resilience, my little cohort of surfing cancer patients proves the ocean is not just a sanctuary, but an active prescription for healing.

    But you don’t have to be a surfer to reap the benefits of physical activity during cancer. A new study of 45,530 women published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in September 2026 confirmed what my surf sisters and I already knew: regular exercise gives women going through breast cancer the strength to bounce back more fully and reclaim our lives after treatment. The study followed women for 15 years with data from the Women’s Health Initiative and found that keeping up physical activity and healthy habits prior to a cancer diagnosis acts as a powerful buffer against the physical toll of cancer treatments.

    The trick is to start with small amounts of exercise and work with your care team on a game plan to get active.

    It has been revealed that “Even if you are not an exerciser, you can still start an exercise regimen during chemotherapy,” remarked my oncologist Eva Thomas, MD, from Kaiser Permanente Oakland in California, who encouraged and cheered on my surfing during chemotherapy. “It sounds counter-intuitive, but women tell me that when they push themselves to exercise, they feel better. Mood is better, sleep is better, energy is increased, and body aches are reduced.”.

    In 2022, the American Society of Clinical Oncology released the first-ever exercise guidelines based on more than 100 clinical trials examining the link between exercise and cancer treatment. For anyone going through cancer who wants to get active, the American College of Sports Medicine created a step-by-step guide in 2024 with research benefits and resources. It outlines a path to get started.

    My own path began years before cancer, as a young woman fixated on surfing, who waited decades to act upon her dream.

    It has been revealed that looking back, I see that my surfing community—and the strength and identity it gave me—helped me to charge forward through the scariest chapter of my life. The takeaway lesson is useful for all women and men facing challenges: Don’t delay trying something fresh and scary. It may end up transforming, and saving, you.

    Sources indicate that danielle Cass lives with her husband in Northern California, where they raised their 26-year-old son, 23-year-old daughter, and dogs. When she’s not surfing with friends, she leads Responsible AI enablement at Microsoft. A two-minute short film about her midlife entry into surfing Learning to Surf at 52 screened at the 2022 San Diego Surf Festival. Follow her surfing through cancer adventures on Instagram @danielle.cass and Substack Danielle Rides the Cancer Wave.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A helicopter transports a deceased hiker recovered from Humboldt Peak. (Photo: Custer County Sheriff's Office).

    A hiker who went missing on a Colorado 14er earlier this week was found dead from an apparent fall on November 24, following a three-day search that sent rescuers combing the high country in winter conditions.

    Custer County Search and Rescue (CCSAR) mentioned in a press release that a Colorado Army National Guard helicopter participating in the search spotted “evidence of a fatal fall.” Rescuers were able to confirm the deceased was the missing man, a 31-year-old from the Denver area who CCSAR described as an experienced hiker.

    According to recent reports, authorities noted that the hiker had summited 14,068-foot Humboldt Peak solo early on the morning of Sunday, November 22. At 5 p.m., CCSAR was notified that the hiker still hadn’t returned, and sent teams into the field alongside aerial support from Reach Air and Flight for Life. The missing hiker had shared his strategy with his family; however, while rescuers promptly located his car, they were unable to locate him despite searching through the night in winter weather. Additional ground teams joined the search the following morning, but fared no better.

    After pausing the search for the night, 21 volunteers, including K9 teams and drone operators, returned to the field on Tuesday. During the operation, authorities closed the South Colony area to cars and hikers.

    In a statement, the Custer County Sheriff’s Office offered its condolences to the deceased hiker’s family, friends, and fiancé, and said that both the hiker’s plan and cell phone forensics helped authorities determine where they should look.

    Compared to other 14ers in the same area, the hike up Humboldt is relatively straightforward. The standard West Ridge route follows the feature of the same name roughly 11 miles out and back to the summit. During fall and winter, however, snow and ice can both make it more difficult to stay on-route and increase the consequences of a slip on the peak’s exposed ridgeline. It was not immediately clear which route the hiker took to the summit.

    The nearby South Colony SNOTEL station, which sits at 10,800 feet, recorded 16 inches of snow on the ground on November 22, up nearly 7 inches from the week prior.

    Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors.
    • Chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer.
    • I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors. (Photo: Courtesy Falkenstein Family Collection).

    Chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer. Better known by many as Falky, Finkelstein, Steiny, Schwackenstein, or Commando, Chris wore many hats throughout his life: devoted husband and father, loyal friend, accomplished climber, photographer, skier, whitewater kayaker, windsurfer, mountain biker, self-proclaimed computer nerd, and passionate lover of Yosemite and the outdoors.

    I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport. I enjoyed it, but pursued other sports. In a way, I don’t think I’ve found a climbing partner that was ever as dialed as he was. My Dad was so quiet and humble about his achievements; there were so many things he never mentioned. I remember being out climbing with him, when he would tell some story like, “We were out here in the ‘80s, blasting a boom box and climbing.” It turns out, he would be talking about a first ascent.

    Those who knew him will remember his adventurous spirit, his enthusiasm for life, and the joy he found in exploring the world around him. His love for the outdoors was infectious. And the memories he created along the way will live on in those fortunate enough to have shared in his adventures.

    It has been revealed that when Chris arrived in Yosemite in 1972, he brought a foundation of climbing experience from the Gunks of Newly introduced York. His natural athleticism, determination, and enthusiasm quickly drew him into the dynamic and evolving climbing scene of Yosemite Valley. What began as an introduction to the Yosemite climbing community grew into a lifelong passion and a lasting legacy.

    He once remarked, “So off I went at 18 to explore climbing in Yosemite. Best decision of my life, and a true highlight… I consider my life beginning after 18. Stay young at heart forever if you can.”.

    It has been revealed that chris spent the remainder of his life in and around Yosemite, calling many places home over the years, including Camp 4, the Annex, Badger Pass, Sonora, Tuolumne Meadows, and El Portal. Eventually, he settled in Foresta, where he and his wife, Doe, retired to the home they built together.

    In a recent development, throughout his years in Yosemite, Chris became a respected presence in the climbing community, known for being a quiet and humble force. He established multiple first ascents in Yosemite Valley and Tuolumne Meadows. Among his notable first ascents were Do or Fly (5.11c), The Speed of Life (5.11b), Black Angel (5.11a), and Highway Star (5.10a). Along with Don Reid, he co-authored Rock Climbs of Tuolumne Meadows, first published in 1983. Four additional editions later followed. He also authored Yosemite Sport Climbs in 1992. Through his climbs, guidebooks, and contributions to the community, Chris helped shape and document Yosemite’s rich climbing history.

    It has been revealed that beyond his physical accomplishments in climbing, he inspired others and expanded the appreciation for the outdoors through his photography, videography, and online content. He captured the many aspects of climbing, mountaineering, and skiing, while sharing the extraordinary beauty of Yosemite.

    Recent findings suggest that chris’s work appeared in a wide range of publications, climbing guides, gear catalogs, climbing films, commercials, Hollywood productions, and websites. Chris’s photography became a familiar part of the Yosemite landscape itself. As Don Reid once remarked with a teasing smirk, “You know you are made with Yosemite photography when your photos appear on the Coke machines, shuttle buses, and climbing guide covers of the place.”.

    It has been revealed that when it was too cold to climb, Chris also had a deep love for winter sports. He played hockey throughout his life and contributed to the local pick up hockey club in Yosemite. Alongside Bruce Brossman and Loyd Price, Chris completed the first single-day trans-Sierra ski trip via Tioga Pass. His name also lives on through several first descents in the Sierras, including the Solstice Couloir and Powerhouse Chute.

    It has been revealed that at Badger Pass Ski Resort, Chris spent many years serving as ski patrol manager. He brought his knowledge of climbing techniques into ski patrol training, developing methods for chairlift rescues and assisting with backcountry rescue efforts. His impact was perhaps best captured by a skier he helped, who later described him as “an angel emerging from the woods.”.

    Early in his career, Chris worked for the Yosemite Climbing School, teaching climbing during the summer months and cross-country skiing in winter. He enjoyed summers as the employee housing manager in Tuolumne Meadows. In retirement, Chris continued to explore and enjoy the Sierras, while taking great pride in perfecting the art of being a grandfather. Chris also became an unofficial voice of Yosemite locals, keeping friends and former park residents connected to the place they loved by sharing updates and insights into the ever-changing landscape of Yosemite.

    Chris loved everything Yosemite. He devoted much of his time to documenting not only the climbing, skiing, and athletic pursuits that made the park famous, but also its immense beauty, extensive history, and the development and change over time. With an eye for the extraordinary as well as the everyday, he captured the moments, places, and details that might otherwise go unnoticed. Through his lens and storytelling, Chris shared his deep appreciation for Yosemite. In so doing, he preserved a piece of its story for others.

    Chris is survived by his wife Doe, his son Alex, his daughter-in-law Danielle, and his two-and-a-half-year-old grandson Finn, who loves trying to climb up anything in his path.

    #159445. You’ve Heard “Be Bold, Start Cold.” But How Cold is Too Cold?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1158 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

    You’ve Heard “Be Bold, Start Cold.” But How Cold is Too Cold?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning.
    • Industry observers note that but how cold is too cold?
    • When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Alex Ratson/Getty Images).

    It has been revealed that hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning. On its surface, it’s simple: Don’t bother wearing a ton of layers you’ll take off the first fifteen minutes into your walk. Starting a little colder means skipping the first half mile shed and letting your body naturally warm up to its resting active temperature.

    Industry observers note that but how cold is too cold? How do you tell the difference between a chill that’ll wear off by the first switchback and a sign you should’ve kept your jacket on? Does the first fifteen minutes warming up do more harm than good?

    When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance.

    Recent findings suggest that tipton has spent four decades studying how the body regulates its temperature, and part of his research looks at what happens to hands and feet during prolonged exposure to cold. His studies have informed the British Royal Navy’s approach to cooling overheated officers, and he’s worked with the U.S. Coast Guard to develop a model that estimates how long someone lost at sea might survive in cold water.

    His advice for hikers was simple: have a smart layering strategy. He didn’t take issue with “Be Bold,” but thought hikers should take more care when it comes to starting cold.

    Recent findings suggest that so how do you tell whether you’re underdressed or overprepared? We talked to Tipton, Appalachian Mountain Club guide Marielle Fibish, and western North Carolina search and rescue team member Nancy East about what to wear for the first mile of a winter hike, how to tell when it’s time to add or shed a layer, and when you’re better off starting warm.

    It has been revealed that for East, a good starting point is how you feel while you’re waiting for a hiking partner to lace up their boots. Can you stand around comfortably for a few minutes? “It’s the type of chill that fresh clothes from the dryer would immediately quell,” she notes.

    Tipton suggests paying attention to your hands. As your body cools, blood flow to your fingers decreases, which can make something as simple as working a zipper harder. In his view, “the ideal place to be is where your extremities feel warm, but you’re not producing vast amounts of sweat.”.

    Sources indicate that once you’re walking, pay attention to which way things are headed. Is that slight chill wearing off, or are your fingers getting colder with every switchback?

    “If my hands are getting cold, I’m shivering, or I’m not generating enough body heat to feel comfortable after several minutes of hiking, I’ll add a layer,” East indicates.

    Recent findings suggest that when Fibish gets dressed for a winter hike in the White Mountains, she checks the forecast, then dresses as though it’s about 10°F warmer. Say it’s 20°F at the trailhead. Fibish dresses the way she would for a walk in 30°F weather. The puffy, shell, and extra mittens are all coming with her. They just get to ride in her bag for the first mile.

    One mistake Fibish sees is hikers reaching for the same outfit they’d wear to the ski hill.

    Recent findings suggest that “Insulated snow pants and jackets are great for downhill skiing and making snowmen, but they can be too warm for other outdoor winter activities like hiking or Nordic skiing,” she says. For hiking, she builds her outfit around a close-fitting wool top and bottoms, with hiking or soft-shell pants over the base layer. A separate fleece gives her some warmth she can shed on the first climb without losing her protection from the wind.

    According to recent reports, fibish also thinks about who’s coming along. If you’re breaking trail for the group, you might be glad you left your fleece in your pack. If you tend to run cold and expect to spend some of that first mile waiting for friends, you might want to keep it on. Give yourself five or ten minutes of walking, Fibish indicates, and you’ll have a better sense of how well you guessed.

    For Fibish, the first cue to lose a layer is a little tingle of warmth building under her clothes. Sometimes slipping off her hat or hiking in glove liners is enough. On a sustained climb, she might stop to take off her fleece. As Tipton explains, your working muscles produce heat. Taking off a layer lets more of that heat escape into the air, so your body can regulate its core temperature with less sweating.

    Your hands can tell you when it’s time to add a layer, too. As your body cools, Tipton explains, blood vessels near the skin narrow to conserve heat in your core. That leaves less warm blood flowing to your fingers. East pays attention when her hands start getting colder, even if she’s still walking. She’ll also pull on a layer if she starts to shiver or if several minutes of hiking haven’t warmed her up. “I don’t wait until I’m genuinely cold to do something about it,” she notes.

    A snack break is one layer change you can see coming. Once you stop climbing, your muscles produce less heat, but sweat evaporating from your damp shirt keeps cooling you. If the wind picks up at the top, East pulls on a fleece or puffy, followed by a windproof layer, before she settles in to eat. Jacket first, sandwich second.

    East likes to know what those first ten minutes of walking are going to look like. If it’s especially cold, wet, or windy, she’ll start a little warmer. Same goes for an exposed stretch of trail: If the climb starts somewhere on the other side of a windy meadow, you’ve still got the meadow to cross. You can take your jacket off when you get into an area with more coverage.

    So is “be bold, start cold” good advice? If you’re about to head uphill and you know you’ll be peeling off your fleece by the first switchback, sure. If you’re already cold standing there, you can keep it on and blueprint to stop a few minutes up the trail.

    Sources indicate that on early starts in the Himalayas, Tipton’s group would stop five minutes up the trail so everyone could adjust their layers. It’s advice worth taking. Pick a spot a few minutes up the trail while everyone’s still gearing up. That way, nobody has to be the first to ask, “Mind if I stop and take this thing off?”.

    East has her own version of the phrase: “Start cool, but don’t stay cold.”.

    #159443. Breaking: A Very Serious Story About Falling Asleep While Belaying

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1140 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: A Very Serious Story About Falling Asleep While Belaying

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans.
    • It has been revealed that big falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope.
    • This old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans. (Photo: Mitra Samavaki / Getty).

    It has been revealed that big falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope. Why? With loose rock, aerated ice, and an often minimalist rack, falling off—even with a tight belay—usually spells disaster. A climber has every reason to follow the old “the leader cannot fall” ethos.

    This old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies. This 1,400-meter ice and mixed route began easily enough, with a hike up a hard-packed snow slope at 6 a.m. toward the deep cleft that marked the start. Neither my partner Rory nor I were burdened with rope management during the first hour of climbing, since our rope stayed neatly coiled in a pack.

    Hundreds of meters higher, below one of the crux pitches, we flaked out our rope. Above us stood a terribly skinny pillar of ice no wider than my shoulders at its base. Blue light filtered through its entirety, a sign of its youth and untrustworthiness.

    “I don’t think I should place a screw in that,” Rory decided.

    Sources indicate that I scanned the shattered quartzite behind the pillar, hoping to at least keep us attached to the mountain before Rory essentially soloed the pitch. Two nervous pitons and a shallow micro nut were all I could cobble together after 10 minutes of searching. I stomped out a waist-deep hole in the snow on the back side of the pillar and clipped into our wobbly anchor. My now four-piece anchor—plus Rory’s unshakeable climbing ability—gave us great odds of surviving his lead.

    Industry observers note that the runout pitch gave me ample opportunity to pay out slack as I pleased while munching on trail mix and rehydrating from our busy morning. After all, Rory was not allowed to fall, so he didn’t.

    Falling has been a frowned-upon practice for most of climbing’s history, especially before sport climbing became popular in the 1980s. Only relatively recently, and only in some styles of climbing, have leader falls become no longer taboo—even acceptable and encouraged.

    It has been revealed that the crusty old-timer in me knows that, in any form of free climbing, it is always safer to climb to the top of a pitch without testing your equipment, be it a skinny rope, crashpad, or ice screw. This gut instinct evolved from a time when climbing gear was not completely trustworthy. Maybe you hand-stitched your quickdraw’s webbing yourself. Maybe you’d sourced your climbing protection from a hardware store. Or maybe you had tied your lead line around your waist because drop-seat harnesses hadn’t been invented yet. In this era—really only a few decades ago—your climbing ability was the first line of defense. Ropes and harnesses and removable protection served merely as dubious back-ups.

    But the advent of regular whippers is a tragedy for one more reason: With newfangled belay devices, hang dogging, and constant pleas to “watch me,” belaying has become a real pain in the ass.

    Recent findings suggest that nearly 12 hours later, Rory and I were still on Mount Temple. We’d topped out the ice climbing portion of the face and traversed across open snow slopes and through rock bands to a final serrated crux: the Black Towers. Countless turrets of dark limestone slice across the summit ridge of Mount Temple, creating difficult route finding even on a clear summer’s day. We were approaching midnight in November and a thick fog had choked the upper mountain. Visibility hovered around 10 meters. I had no idea where we were supposed to go.

    Industry observers note that thankfully it was Rory’s lead again, and he was questing. Fifteen minutes ticked by as he wandered up a steep rocky groove, then another 15 of the rope unmoving. An hour passed. I clicked off my headlamp to save battery. More time passed. I figured I could tie off the rope and catch a few Zs, so I did. Sleep felt amazing. I was glad that even as we approached 24 hours on the move, Rory still knew the rules: The leader cannot fall. And the belayer gets to sleep.

    I woke up to the sound of Rory’s voice. He’d been blocked by an overhang and was downclimbing. Thick, icy fog obscured our vision as I took the rack and traversed along a snow ledge looking for easier passage. The fog would sometimes lift for an instant—I’d spot a lonely star above—and I’d frantically flick my headlamp to full strength to catch a glimpse of the mountain. But before my eyes could adjust to the fresh sight, the fog would crash back in like a breaking wave, drowning us in uncertainty once again.

    In a recent development, this story does not end in a climbing success. We did not ultimately find our way through the Black Towers, nor did we share a weary, satisfied hug on the summit of Mount Temple. We became lost and a little delirious on a large mountain in the middle of the night and needed to go down.

    We stayed roped together as we retraced our steps through deep snow on the upper mountain. I was a little worried about triggering an avalanche, but mainly I was just exhausted. If I stumbled, I would prefer to slide 30 meters before being caught by the rope than well over a thousand into the next life.

    Industry observers note that rory and I regrouped at an anchor I’d built in an outcrop of yellow rock. He led out across another snowfield which terminated at a gigantic notch in an otherwise sheer ridgeline. The notch marked the start of a classic ski descent, the 60-degree Aemmer Couloir, and our escape hatch. Rory trudged toward it and I paid out rope, nodding off again.

    In a recent development, suddenly, I was awake. I had not pooped all day, yet the kilogram of trail mix and sausage and cheese I’d downed was making a basement appearance.

    According to recent reports, “Rory! Do you need a real belay for this bit? I really need to poo,” I yelled into the fog.

    “No, I don’t care,” the fog yelled back.

    I let the rope feed through the anchor, then unclipped it from my belay device and, without moving even a step away from our anchor, unloaded into the snow bank.

    It would have been a disgusting mess had Rory fallen and weighted the anchor, dragging me into my own steaming waste. But he didn’t, and I made it back to civilization with both my dignity and my life intact.

    Congress Just Voted to Redraw Yosemite National Park Boundaries. The Bill Is Heading to Trump’s Desk.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (478 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).
    • A fresh law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.
    • It has been revealed that on November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).

    A fresh law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.

    It has been revealed that on November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S. Senator Alex Padilla and Republican U.S. Representative Tom McClintock, both from California.

    If the president signs it into law, the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act will transfer 160 acres of Stanislaus National Forest land to the NPS for management as part of Yosemite. Another 170 acres of Yosemite National Park land will be transferred to the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) for management as part of Stanislaus National Forest.

    The decision comes after a flurry of debate following announcements for public land swaps and transfers. An August report alleged that the NPS was attempting to execute a land exchange within Yosemite for a private road, which reportedly would have given property within park boundaries to a Nevada-based real estate firm. Then, in September, Major League Baseball approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at Grand Teton National Park in northwest Wyoming.

    Recent findings suggest that lawmakers say the Ackerson Meadow decision will address a problem in federal land management in the Sierra Nevada: the checkerboard of boundary lines. In 2016, the Trust for Public Land bought the 400-acre Ackerson Meadow parcel and gifted it to Yosemite. However, the chunk was almost completely surrounded by the Stanislaus National Forest with very little contiguous border to the park itself, lawmakers said.

    “Ackerson Meadow is one of the most critical wildlife corridors in our state, yet the current configuration of the region puts habitat conservation at risk,” Padilla noted in a statement. “This land transfer is a simple and beneficial exchange that will help protect endangered wildlife, mitigate wildfire threats, and sustain our rural economy.”.

    It has been revealed that jackie McGuinness, Padilla’s communications director, told Outside that the agreement will change Yosemite’s boundaries. A map McGuinness sent demonstrates the park boundaries shifting to the east, filling in a checkerboard pattern left blocked out by the previous perimeter lines.

    According to recent reports, USFS manages land ranchers use for livestock grazing on national forests and grasslands, while the NPS restricts most of these operations within park boundaries. The land exchange between the two agencies eliminates confusion caused by the jurisdictional split, McClintock noted in a U.S. House floor statement on September 14.

    “The proposed land exchange would make that cooperative approach easier by eliminating the confusion caused by split jurisdiction,” he mentioned. “Ranchers need to know where their permits apply, where infrastructure can be maintained, and who is responsible for decisions affecting their operations.”.

    It’s unclear whether or when Trump intends to sign the bill into law.

    According to recent reports, there’s nothing more delightful than rummaging around in an oversized sock to find a piece of backpacking gear you never knew you needed. Even if your giftee isn’t overwhelmed with joy (we’re sure they will be), these micro-gifts won’t set you back like an expensive, ill-fitting sleeping bag might. From energy chews to our current favorite pocket knife, here are ten backpacker-tested stocking stuffers, all small enough to fit into a hipbelt pocket.

    According to recent reports, hydration and electrolytes are a stacked category, but we love that Tailwind uses easy-to-drink, naturally-flavored mixes instead of unpronounceable ingredients. The 25-serving bulk bag is a good economical choice, but if single-serving packets are more convenient, you can opt for a variety pack instead. For super sweaty hikers, Saltt drink mixes add a dose of sodium to the blend without making it taste like seawater.

    Hiking hard in the heat can be a recipe for an upset stomach, but hikers still have to eat enough to power their miles. Skratch’s energy chews are some of the easiest to get down thanks to the varied texture of the sour sugar coating and punchy flavors. Choose between caffeinated and non-caffeinated varieties, all with easy-to-digest carbs for a quick boost of energy that doesn’t entail gnawing on a dense protein bar.

    A headband might not seem like a thrilling gift, but no one is ever sad they threw it into their pack. Smartwool’s version is warm and wicking, blocking brisk winds around the forehead with a windproof panel and extra width around the ears for coverage. This is the perfect accessory for chilly-but-not-frigid hikes where a beanie is overkill, but the wind is turning your forehead into an ice cube.

    Sources indicate that leatherman might be best known for its ranch-ready multitools, but it also has a lovely line of reliable, lightweight pocket knives. The Skeletool KB weighs just over one ounce, has a built-in bottle opener, and a tensioned belt clip for securing to a pocket or an interior flap on your pack. We’ve carried this for weeks at a time without seeing any dulling or corrosion. If you want to go significant, you can also spring for a high-end Benchmade Bugout Knife, which weighs 1.85 ounces and has a range of customization options.

    It has been revealed that remember being a kid and groaning when you got socks for Christmas? Those days are long gone—we don’t know any hiker who isn’t thrilled to unwrap a fresh pair of wool socks. These trail-ready socks have a moderate amount of cushioning and structure for support without feeling compressive. Made with 75-percent merino, they also have excellent odor-resistance and softness while still holding their shape.

    In a recent development, hydraPak has made impressive strides in its line of ultralight, packable filters in the past few years. This filter-and-bottle combination uses their flagship soft flask with one of our favorite hollow-fiber filters. The flow rate stays strong and fast for longer than other similar styles, and the tough, seam-welded TPU bottle can withstand a whole lot of squeezing. The wide mouth makes it easy to fill, and hikers can either squeeze it into a larger bottle for drinking water or drink directly from the filter.

    Black Diamond nailed it with this headlamp. The Astro 300 offers an excellent combination of low weight (just 2.65 ounces), night-hiker-approved 300-lumen output, and a conveniently integrated rechargeable battery, all at a reasonable price. It’s highly waterproof and durable for long, rugged outings, and the single button is easy to press while wearing gloves. The only downside is that it doesn’t include a red light. If that’s an issue, Nitecore’s UT27 MCT Pro 800 is more expensive, but weighs the same and comes with a red light option.

    Though it gets less press than rolled ankles and bad knees, skin chafing is the sneaky destroyer of many good days on the trail. Keep your hiker’s inner thighs safe with a stick of Squirrel’s Nut Butter, which has a trimmed-down formula limited to natural ingredients like coconut oil, cocoa butter, and Vitamin E oil. It glides on smoothly, and each application lasts several hours. Fast-packers and people in more humid environments might also appreciate Run Slick, which has a roll-on formula that is among the most sweat-resistant we’ve ever tested.

The brand uses single-origin beans from farms in Colombia, and each packet is perfect for 8-10 ounces of water.

We love the convenience of having one less thing to charge on the trail, and this pair from Skullcandy has excellent sound quality for a reasonable price. They’re also durable: The cords on our pair have survived over a month of daily use on-trail without separating. If you’re looking to splurge, Bose recently updated its flagship wired earbuds, and the bump in price gets you better noise-canceling and a clear in-line microphone for ordering pizza to the trailhead.

    #159439. Put Your Rock Shoes in the Oven—You’ll Thank Us

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (620 w)

    Put Your Rock Shoes in the Oven—You’ll Thank Us

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A pinhole image of a person peering into their oven at home.
    • In a recent development, I grew up in a gym.
    • According to recent reports, if there’s one thing that has held true over my years of cramming my feet into tiny, downturned rock shoes for the sake of performance, it’s that breaking in shoes sucks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A pinhole image of a person peering into their oven at home. (Photo: Getty Images).

    In a recent development, I grew up in a gym. I learned my first curse words on a chalky, sweat-stained gym mat. I got my first tattoo with the friends I did four-by-fours with. First boyfriend, even.

    According to recent reports, if there’s one thing that has held true over my years of cramming my feet into tiny, downturned rock shoes for the sake of performance, it’s that breaking in shoes sucks. Every time, no getting around it, a horrible experience. During one gym session, a friend noted she’d pay to have someone break in her shoes for her. We were the same size, and I was pretty desperate for money at the time—but still, some things just aren’t worth it. And when you not only have to break in the shoes, but have a double training session ahead of you while your feet are screaming with pain? I’m sure that I cried once over it.

    It has been revealed that when the pandemic hit, suddenly I wasn’t going to the gym anymore. And because—at least at the beginning—nobody was sure about transmission via holds outside, I refrained from climbing rock as well. During that turbulent time, a funny thing happened: Either my feet flattened out or my tolerance for tiny shoes decreased. Because when gyms reopened and I tried to push myself through the break-in process again, suddenly it felt a lot more hateful.

    As I complained loudly (and probably all while looking desperate) at Monkey House Carbondale in December 2020, a local friend, the pro climber Dan Mirsky, overheard me.

    “Try putting ‘em in the oven,” he said.

    It has been revealed that “No way. They’ll delaminate!” I protested.

    In a recent development, “No, seriously. Just for a few minutes on the lowest setting. Game-changer.”.

    It has been revealed that I took his tip, which I later learned he had originally gotten from another pro climber, Jonathan Siegrist, to heart. That night, I set up my station: oven, on the lowest setting (170 degrees), timer, and area on the carpet where I would dance around like a circus monkey. In the shoes went, for two minutes. I would then wear them for five to ten minutes—pacing, with some good ol’ fashioned calf raises mixed in—and then they’d go back in the oven, for another cycle or two. (Note: This only works with a standard oven, not a microwave—do not microwave your rock shoes or it will severely damage/deform them!).

    I couldn’t believe the results. Those brand-upcoming puppies felt more akin to the pair you sweated in all summer and have yet to send to a resoler (God bless the person who has to touch that pair). It was one of those moments when you realize your life has changed forever.

    In a recent development, and a fun fact for you, which I learned with more research: Leather stretches when wet (duh!). So try the oven thing, plus adding a sprinkling of water when they shoes are still hot, prior to donning them. And voilà! Your warm, wet shoes will slide right on and stretch even more.

    Curious for his take, I reached out to Siegrist. “Yes, I do that sometimes!” he wrote. “Not as much any more, because I think I just simply get bigger shoes. Ha!”.

    And that, actually, might just be the best tip of all.

    Note: While the author has successfully applied this tip on multiple occasions, as has Siegrist and Mirsky, not all shoemakers recommend. Scarpa, for example, has noted that this method of breaking in shoes will reduce glue strength and void shoe warranty.

    #159438. Tech Report: Skiing Takes a Toll on Your Knees. Here’s the Muscle You Need to Strengthen, According to an Orthopedic Surgeon.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1072 w)

    Tech Report: Skiing Takes a Toll on Your Knees. Here’s the Muscle You Need to Strengthen, According to an Orthopedic Surgeon.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Photo: Monster walk exercise: Erstudiostok/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva).
    • Strong legs are essential for skiing without injury.
    • According to recent reports, that means the smaller guys often get neglected.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Monster walk exercise: Erstudiostok/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva).

    Strong legs are essential for skiing without injury. But many traditional strength training programs focus on the bigger muscles in your lower half, including the quads, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus (your largest butt muscle).

    According to recent reports, that means the smaller guys often get neglected. And one small guy in particular, the gluteus medius, which forms part of your side butt, is worth paying attention to if you actually want to reduce your risk of knee pain and injury this winter.

    Because ACL tears are among the most common ski injuries, Dr. Gregory Lichtman, an orthopedic surgeon in northern California and a physician for the U.S. women’s ski team, puts heavy emphasis on strengthening the glute medius. In his view, it’s one of the most vital muscles for staying safe and skiing well.

    Unfortunately, even high-level athletes can have a weak glute medius, according to Lichtman. That’s because unlike the quads, hamstrings, calves, and glute max—which can naturally get strong from activities like road running and hill climbing—the glute medius typically needs to be intentionally strengthened.

    Read on to learn why this small muscle is so key, Lichtman’s favorite way to strengthen it, and other essential fitness tips for injury prevention.

    The glute medius is a small muscle on your outer hip that fires up when you bring your leg out to the side, a motion known as hip abduction. It also helps control the knee by preventing it from caving inward (a position known as valgus) as you perform various movements. And it assists you in balancing on one leg, which is important when loading your downhill ski, Lichtman says.

    In skiing, if you get into the back seat (meaning, you shift your body weight backward, instead of staying centered over your skis) and the knee goes into valgus, the tibia can internally rotate, “and that’s where the ACL tears occur,” Lichtman states. Even if you don’t get a full-blown ACL tear, going into valgus when you ski can contribute to patellofemoral pain syndrome, a fancy term for pain at the front of the kneecap, Lichtman says.

    By strengthening the glute medius, you can make it more resistant to valgus in the first place, which decreases your chances of both ACL tears and general knee pain.

    There are also performance benefits: “A strong gluteus medius also really allows you to stand on your downhill ski a little bit more aggressively and really make a more aggressive turn,” Lichtman says. That’s because when you place most of your weight on your downhill ski (the one that’s closest to the bottom of the hill), your G-forces will want to throw you down the mountain. But having a strong glute medius, in addition to strong quads and core muscles, helps form a strong pillar on your outer hip, which “really allows you to withstand those G-forces the best,” Lichtman says.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the classic ways to target the glute medius is to strap on ankle weights, lie on your side, and lift and lower your top leg. Lichtman claims. This exercise can absolutely strengthen your glute medius, but it’s not Lichtman’s go-to. That’s because it primarily just isolates that muscle and doesn’t mimic how we move in sports.

    It has been revealed that A better bet, Lichtman says, is to focus on exercises that simultaneously activate the gluteus medius and other muscle groups because that better resembles how we use this muscle during athletics. His favorite exercise that ticks that box? The monster walk. Not only does this move really fire up the gluteus medius, but it also works the core, hamstrings, quads, and glute max, he says.

    Industry observers note that incorporate this exercise into your workouts three days a week, with at least one day off between sessions so the muscle has the downtime it needs to recover and build back stronger. To stave off boredom and also work different parts of your hips and quads, incorporate different variations of the monster walk throughout the week. For example, instead of stepping straight out to the side, step forward and back, or diagonally forward and diagonally back. As long as you have good form and keep your legs spread apart so that you feel tension from the band the whole time, “all directions can be effective,” Lichtman indicates.

    Recent findings suggest that lichtman suggests doing monster walks during both pre-season and throughout ski season. “One of the significant pitfalls is that we will all get ready for ski season, and then taper off our dry land training,” he explains. “If you’re one of the fortunate few who can ski five or six days a week, you’re probably getting enough exercise, and you probably don’t want to stress your body out any more than that. But for those of us who are skiing two to three days a week, finding some time to do some cross-training and continue to work on our core and our hip abductor strength is really key because those are the less commonly used muscles during skiing.”.

    Once this exercise becomes easy, level up the challenge by using a stronger resistance band.

    Sources indicate that A strong glute medius can keep you safe on the slopes. But it’s not the only fitness-related aspect of injury prevention.

    According to recent reports, A strong core and quads, along with good overall endurance, are also key. That’s because one of the essential components of an ACL tear pattern in skiing is getting kicked into the back seat. And while the gluteus medius helps guard against knee valgus in this position, it doesn’t prevent you from getting into the back seat in the first place, Lichtman explains. What does help? Having strong core and quad muscles, plus overall endurance. This trifecta, Lichtman notes, is “fundamental” to staying out of the back seat.

    It has been revealed that on the endurance front, the goal is to be as fresh after lunch as you are after breakfast, Lichtman says. “Fatigue is definitely a risk factor for ACL tears,” he says, explaining that fatigued skiers more frequently get into the back seat and sustain injuries than those who aren’t zapped. So make sure your dryland training doesn’t just focus on lifting weights: “A balance of endurance and strength training is integral for a skier preparing for ski season,” Lichtman says.

    Latest Update: The Six Formative Moments in Every Climbing Career

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1274 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Placing your first cam is a memorable, and often horrifying, moment in every climber's career.
    • In a recent development, every climber has experienced a truly unforgettable moment.
    • According to recent reports, not all climbers will share these exact memories, but there are some key moments that define almost every climbing career.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Placing your first cam is a memorable, and often horrifying, moment in every climber's career. (Photo: Andrew Burr).

    In a recent development, every climber has experienced a truly unforgettable moment. For some, it’s tagging that tree after climbing the Nose. For others, it’s the vast bulk of Denali filling the windshield of the de Havilland Otter. For yet others still, it’s that first splitter at Indian Creek, that first wide crack at Vedauwoo, or that first roof at the Shawangunks.

    According to recent reports, not all climbers will share these exact memories, but there are some key moments that define almost every climbing career. Whether you’re a climber from Southern California or from Northern Vietnam, these will probably be familiar, and they probably changed the way you do business. They’re rites of passage, and when newer climbers pass through those same gates, you’ll grin knowingly, nod your head and say “Shit, we’ve all been there!”.

    These days, just about every climber gets started indoors, and the transition from gym to crag is a big deal. When you tentatively emerge from the womb of the climbing gym, the possibilities of ascending ACTUAL ROCKS are infinite and exhilarating. There you are with your laminated lead card still attached to your harness, squinting and blinking in the unfamiliar sunlight, craning your neck ever upward under a vast sea of stone….

    On closer inspection, you see them—occasionally chalked, but devoid of color, tape, or any visual aid that would denote a route. This is concerning, and your consternation only deepens as you pull on. What follows is a desperate pumpfest during which you grasp ineffectively at every possible (and impossible) hold, ignore your footwork, and mutter phrases like “Is this one on?” and “5.9, my ass.”.

    Recent findings suggest that now, I realize that several crusty veterans are about to flood the comments section with hardcore tales from the pre-gym era—how the closest they’ve ever come to touching plywood was hammering home-slung timber chocks into cracks, how much of the Earth’s granite was still cooling in subterranean caverns when they started climbing, how their favorite Triceratop died of exhaustion during a regular 16-day approach. Sure, not every climbing career began with a heady gym to crag transition, but the impertinent youths whose did would agree—we’ve all been there.

    You’re inching left on a sketchy traverse when your belayer blasts you with an unsolicited beta spray.

    “Watch that rope, dude. It’s behind your leg.”.

    Recent findings suggest that but you don’t got this, and when your foot pops and that tenuous crimp unlatches, you fall. The rope catches mid-calf and suddenly you’re upside-down and giving the wall the old “Glasgow Kiss”—a headbutt, in other words. Wear a helmet, kids. After righting yourself and lowering to the ground, it’s not entirely clear what hurts more: that throbbing, rope-shaped welt fused with tiny purple and yellow fibers or your pride.

    Nope, it’s definitely your pride, but you can salve your damaged ego with the knowledge that almost every climber suffers the indignity of a super-ugly-upside-down-leg-behind-the-rope whipper at some point. Most will only suffer it once, because this hard-knock lesson improves rope management which makes for better, safer lead climbing. Don’t feel too bad, you’re not alone in making this rookie mistake. We’ve all been there.

    Sources indicate that it might happen on that 5.9 you’ve climbed more times than you’ve had hot dinners, or perhaps on the tail end of a 12-hour minor epic. Either way, as you prepare to lower or rappel, you notice that something is not quite right. Scratch that—it’s horrifically wrong. You’re not clipped in properly, and had you have weighted the system, you’d have taken the Big Ride.

    In the days and weeks following this potentially fatal near-miss, make a serious review of your systems. The experience should form a powerful lesson—almost as powerful as the gastro-intestinal evacuations that occurred after the bad taco you ate in El Potrero Chico.

    Complacency and fatigue are often factors, but the true reason for serious human error is this: Your systems suck. Maybe you’re weren’t applying best practice, or maybe you’re not consistent enough with those that you do use. A smart (or sufficiently chastened) climber will embrace this opportunity to analyze, criticize, and ultimately improve techniques, because although we’ve all been there, it’s not somewhere we wish to return.

    There comes a time in a climber’s life when they must place a piece of traditional protection, either by design or by default. Then comes a sudden realization, a piercing moment when it becomes clear that one’s entire being is committed to the inner workings of a spring-loaded camming device or the security of an asymmetrical hunk of aluminum. Eyes glaze over, total recall of high school physics occurs, Rainman-esque calculations of friction coefficients and force vectors take place….

    Industry observers note that this moment is polarizing. It alternately fills climbers with invigoration, or with an existential dread so profound it would make Friedrich Nietzsche look like the Dalai Lama. Climbers then find themselves in one of two camps—either “newly minted trad climber” or “fuck that, never again.” And whichever camp you find yourself in, you’ll probably come to regard the other as having serious and incurable mental deficiencies. But no matter which side of the fence you end up on, we’ve all been there.

    What was that? Oh, nothing. Just your A2 pulley disintegrating, along with your dreams of onsighting The Widowmaker (VI 5.14a X A4 M10ish) at HardBastard Canyon this year. Worse still, it happened in the gym. Oh, the humanity.

    Your first climbing injury comes with two realizations. The first is that your immediate future is going to look a lot different from how you envisaged it five minutes ago. The second is that you’re not invincible. Everybody thinks it can’t happen to them, until it does.

    According to recent reports, the recovery period for a finger injury is horrifically tedious—six ponderous months of pulling ever so gently on holds that are no smaller than the West Buttress of Denali. Afterward, you won’t be able to tear the skin off a custard, but you’ll be a gun at warming up, an ace at stretches, and an absolute legend at taking rest days. But here’s an idea… why not buck the trend and start doing these BEFORE you get injured? We’ve all been there, but if we can prevent it from happening, why do we all wait until it’s too late?

    According to recent reports, belayers are a dime a dozen, but a real climbing partner is a true gift. But what makes a real partner?

    In a recent development, A real partner is just as stoked as you are, if not more so. They don’t say things like “why” and “how much.” They say things like “hell yes” and “let’s do this.” They can spoon you in a bivvy cave without it getting overly weird. They will empty your piss bottle on the understanding that you’ll return the favor sometime. They will lend you that No. 6 without a moment’s hesitation. They really, really want to see you crush that pitch.

    Recent findings suggest that put simply, a real climbing partner is someone you would follow to the ends of the earth, and regularly do. A real climbing partner can turn a bad climb into a good one, a good climb into a great one, and a great climb into a life-changing experience. Forming deep and genuine connections is one of the finest aspects of the sport, and if there is one thing I truly hope, it’s that we’ve all been there.
