    #159435. My Local Trail Is Crumbling. Should I Fix It Without Approval?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1960 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    My Local Trail Is Crumbling. Should I Fix It Without Approval?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Authorized trail work (like the work shown) is more preferable.
    • It has been revealed that what should you do when your favorite trails aren’t being maintained?
    • Industry observers note that according to the LA Times, the hiker is named Mark Orr.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Authorized trail work (like the work shown) is more preferable. But sometimes hikers do trail repairs on their own. (Photo: Marty Caivano/Getty Images).

    It has been revealed that what should you do when your favorite trails aren’t being maintained? The question was sparked by a recent story in the Los Angeles Times about a concerned hiker who lugged nearly 100 pounds of construction materials up Mount Baldy. The hiker proceeded to install a DIY retaining barrier to widen a crumbling section of trail across a well-known section called Devil’s Backbone in August.

    Industry observers note that according to the LA Times, the hiker is named Mark Orr. On Reddit, some commenters thanked Orr for taking the initiative to improve a popular and dangerous trail, where hikers have fallen to their deaths in the past. Others saw videos of the repairs and raised concerns. Would Orr’s project—constructed from aluminum sheeting, steel wire, and rebar—really hold up against years of erosion and heavy foot traffic?

    Within just a few weeks, runoff carved a deep hole in the dirt below the retaining wall, proving the naysayers right.

    “The first thing is, it was nothing but well-intentioned by somebody who loves the mountain and wants it to be safer for everybody,” Orr told the LA Times. “I totally get that my first crack at this, I didn’t do everything right, and I’m actively working with the San Gabriel Mountains Trailbuilders to get it right before this winter.”.

    As a longtime trail worker, I can’t condone Orr’s trail work on Mount Baldy, even if his heart was in the right place. But after years of building trails and working with volunteers, I also know that unauthorized trail work happens all the time. I’ve seen poorly constructed drainage ditches, wobbly rock staircases, and retaining walls I didn’t trust to hold my body weight.

    In a recent development, I have also seen hikers clearing away brush, pruning branches, and cutting and then removing downed trees that have fallen across the trail. I see people with chainsaws strapped to their dirt bikes or loppers in a side pouch of their backpacks. The work these hikers, cyclists, and dirt bikers do is sometimes illegal. It’s also necessary. Without them, our trails would be in worse shape. And given the state of our public land management agencies, I can’t blame them for choosing to go rogue.

    According to recent reports, but amongst ad hoc trail work, there’s a sliding scale between harmful and helpful. And I have some thoughts on when and where it’s justified to do unsanctioned trail work. Spoiler alert: if you’re planning on building walls, moving boulders, or cutting down trees, you need to go back to the drawing board.

    According to recent reports, one of my friends, a U.S. Forest Service trail manager in Tennessee who asked not to be named in this story, has gone to great lengths to empower local citizens to perform trail work themselves. Thanks to his efforts, volunteers are now certified to use chainsaws on Forest Service land and operate independently. When they come across downed logs or a brushy trail, they don’t have to seek permission to organize a trail maintenance day. They just get to work.

    Sources indicate that unfortunately, not every national forest has the manpower to do this. Land management agencies like the Forest Service and National Park Service are in the midst of unprecedented budget cuts and staffing shortages, and our trails are suffering. Since President Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025, the Forest Service has shed more than 5,000 jobs, including thousands of field-going employees like rangers and trail workers. An internal Forest Service report leaked last year came to a dire conclusion: “Many districts are unable to complete basic trail maintenance. Backcountry trails are being abandoned. Deferred maintenance is exponentially compounding.”.

    According to recent reports, for 2027, Trump is proposing a further 44 percent cut to the Forest Service’s operations budget, which covers employee salaries. The agency has been gutted. Some forest districts no longer have even a single trail worker.

    It has been revealed that the Forest Service indicates that it hopes to offset these challenges through its volunteer program, which it overhauled in 2024. But the agency is now so decimated that some districts can’t even provide mandatory training to volunteers. If you’re a would-be volunteer hoping to use a chainsaw to clear your favorite Forest Service trail, you’re supposed to take a three-day training course first. But many ranger districts no longer offer chainsaw training, forcing volunteers to find a non-profit that offers a similar course, which usually means hours of travel and paying for overnight accommodations.

    Despite those challenges, you should reach out to these agencies and local groups before picking up a tool and heading to the trail. In some cases, you can get in touch with the organization, or land manager, that’s legally responsible for trail maintenance, like the city, county, or state parks and recreation department. In other situations, it may be easier to contact a volunteer group that’s already connected with your local land managers.

    Recent findings suggest that “Contacting your local land manager or volunteer group is how you learn the basics,” Sam Donnelly, the acting executive director at the Tahoe Rim Trail Association told Outside. “It also builds goodwill and makes things official. Land managers can sign an individual volunteer agreement with you if there’s no volunteer organization in the area. All of this helps to prove that you want to show up and put in the work.”.

    Donnelly would know. Maintaining the 165-mile Tahoe Rim Trail is a joint effort between the organization he leads and three national forest units, a state park in Nevada, and another non-profit group—not to mention dozens of volunteers.

    According to recent reports, he understands that some people want to speed up the process by doing unsanctioned trail work. But he does not encourage it. “It’s a trust-building thing,” he stated. “We didn’t get here overnight, but we have the impact we do now because we’ve done things the right way.”.

    Even if you’re convinced there’s no one out there maintaining your local trails, you might be pleasantly surprised. A directory of trail groups on Pinkbike  lists over 1,600 organizations in the United States. Shoot your local group an email, and chances are they’ll be happy to put you to work. In areas with established groups, it might take a while until your favorite trail or pet project makes it onto the calendar. But if you show up consistently, take classes and get first aid certified, you can likely become a trip leader and have input on which trails need attention.

    In areas where trails are more remote and less trafficked, volunteer trail work is often a more casual affair. My mother, a lifetime hiker who lives in central Pennsylvania, was handed a pair of loppers and told she was in charge of maintaining a three-mile section of the Mid-State Trail—without any oversight—on her very first day as a volunteer. All it took was one email and a 15-minute demonstration, and she was official.

    It has been revealed that even if a volunteer group in your area isn’t very active, it’s probably worth reaching out. A group might not have enough active members to strategy work trips, but could still provide valuable intel. They can connect you with land managers, loan you tools, or give you keys to unlock gates for quicker trail access. Plus, your volunteer hours may count towards them receiving a funding grant in the future.

    If you’re truly unable to work with a land manager or volunteer group, I believe there are times when unauthorized trail work is the right choice, even if it is prohibited by the letter of the law.

    According to recent reports, trail work exists on a spectrum in terms of complexity. The most complicated tasks, like building bridges, erecting retaining walls, and constructing fresh trails from scratch, are really engineering projects. The simplest tasks, like trimming back overgrown brush, require almost no training. Most trail work exists in a gray area between these two extremes.

    It has been revealed that complex trail-building projects are not the place to be doing unauthorized trail work. For one thing, they’re often far more involved than most people realize. Even building a small retaining wall takes a lot of effort. The rock or lumber used in the wall generally extends far underground, and is reinforced with rebar and lag screws. The structure is filled with tons of crushed rock and dirt. Staircases, water bars, grade dips, and switchbacks are all similarly complex projects.

    According to recent reports, “Trail building, just the science of it, has come a really long way,” Donnelly said. “There’s a lot more thought put into it than you’d expect. A retaining wall is a good example. It takes weeks to build one so that it will last a hundred years. A normal person who thinks they can just go out and do trail work on their own is probably just creating more work for the people who come after.”.

    Even if you think you know what you’re doing, you could expose yourself to legal trouble by taking on serious trail improvements without approval. Rerouting even a small section of trail often requires an environmental review, as does building a new bridge or boardwalk. You could build a perfect retaining wall, and land managers will still remove it to comply with the rules and regulations they must follow. If you’re interested in this kind of work, you need to volunteer with an official organization.

    It might not be glamorous, but the dead-simple tasks like pruning and cutting branches are really the only ones appropriate for unofficial trail work. The main reason for this is that routine maintenance doesn’t change a trail’s character. You aren’t deciding whether a new retaining wall is appropriate on a wilderness trail. You aren’t building berms for mountain bikes on a multi-use trail. You aren’t digging ditches across the trail where you think water erosion is an glitch. All you’re doing is restoring the trail to what it is supposed to look like in the first place. As long as you don’t leave “punji sticks”, the sharp stubs that are created when you don’t prune a branch flush to the ground or a limb, it’s hard to go wrong. For myself, that means tossing a small hand saw or pair of loppers in my day pack when I go hiking or riding in areas where I know trail maintenance is spotty. I’ll spend an hour of my time cutting back any brush that touches my body as I walk past.

    It’s boring work, and I rarely finish brushing out an entire trail before I have to move on. I don’t get the same sense of accomplishment from pruning branches as I do from moving boulders to build a staircase or cutting down trees to build a log bridge. But it’s notable work, it’s hard to mess up, and no reasonable land manager would give you grief for doing it. In general, trails won’t disappear when a bridge gives out or a staircase falls apart, so long as the rest of the trail is in good condition. But if the entire length of a trail disappears under brush and downed logs, it might be abandoned entirely, or even removed from official maps. Once a trail is decommissioned, it’s far more difficult and costly to build a new trail to replace it, because new trails require lengthy environmental reviews. Simply put, if you love a trail, doing the easy, routine maintenance to make sure it remains passable is the best thing you can do.

    #159434. The Terminus of the CDT is Now Behind a Border Wall. Here’s What Hikers Can Expect

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (590 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

    The Terminus of the CDT is Now Behind a Border Wall. Here’s What Hikers Can Expect

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year.
    • In a recent development, now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls right now under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA).
    • In November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year. The granite obelisk once stood in the open Chihuahuan Desert, in a remote area visited by few except hikers either starting or ending their journeys. The dirt road approaching it, Commodore Road, was unmaintained and required high-clearance vehicles, limiting access and traffic.

    In a recent development, now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls right now under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA). Government contractors graded and widened the road from 8 feet to 24 feet to accommodate construction vehicles. For now, hikers can still enter the NDA with permission and touch the monument—whether they’re starting northbound or ending their CDT hike. However, security guards will eventually usher them away, out of the construction zone.

    In November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus. Neither had been there since construction began in early 2026.

    Industry observers note that “We wanted to see on the ground what was actually happening and what people were experiencing,” Martinez told Backpacker. She described the scene as “surreal.”.

    Recent findings suggest that arriving at the terminus monument, Martinez and Labert watched as two hikers approached in the distance. The two women, trail names Geisha Girl and Fearless, marched toward them, border walls standing on both sides. In an emotional moment, the teary-eyed hikers walked right up to the monument.

    According to recent reports, “I think if they hadn’t been able to put their hands on the physical monument, even though it was between the two barriers, it would have been devastating,” Martinez remarked. “The importance of having access to that now while it’s under construction is so fundamental.”.

    While these changes are striking to someone like Martinez, who has visited this terminus hundreds of times during her work with the non-profit trail organization, she says she sees a silver lining. The construction traffic is annoying, loud, disruptive, and changes the experience of finishing or starting your CDT hike in a quiet corner of the desert. But the improvements to Commodore Road greatly increase access to the trail’s southern terminus.

    “Building a road invites more people, which means more people can get there, which is a beautiful thing. They can drive their loved ones to the trail and pick them up from the trail much easier than it ever has been,” she stated. But at the same time, the improvements make it feel less remote, and could make it significantly busier. “So it’s bittersweet,” she said.

    Sometime “in the near future,” Martinez said the terminus monument will be moved out of the NDA. Then, the CDTC will create a new one with accurate longitude and latitude markers. She sees that as an opportunity to rethink how the monument will be dedicated and to include indigenous voices that weren’t involved when the original monument was dedicated in 1974.

    Asked what hikers should expect when approaching the southern terminus of the CDT, Martinez paused thoughtfully.

    It has been revealed that “I think they should be prepared for an amazing experience in one of the most beautiful places on the planet,” she mentioned. “But you’re going to see this infrastructure now that didn’t exist before. And I would ask people to lean into the good stuff and then also use that moment as an opportunity to reflect on how the experience is making them feel.”.

    #159433. 9 Moments and Pioneers From the Evolution of Yosemite, in Photos

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (929 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    9 Moments and Pioneers From the Evolution of Yosemite, in Photos

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Perhaps the most recognizable feature of the granite behemoth that is El Capitan is the gigantic diorite streak running right up the middle of the southeast face.
    • It wasn’t until October 1963 when Royal Robbins and Glen Denny began hunting around on the wall.
    • Read this: “The First Ascent of the North America Wall” by Royal Robbins.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Perhaps the most recognizable feature of the granite behemoth that is El Capitan is the gigantic diorite streak running right up the middle of the southeast face. Saped like the North American continent, it’s this route’s namesake. Although this birthmark is visually striking, the brittle black rock it contains and the lack of a clear, natural line kept climbers focused on the more aesthetic and relatively easier southwest face.

    It wasn’t until October 1963 when Royal Robbins and Glen Denny began hunting around on the wall. Eventually, they aided up to about 600 feet. In fall 1964, a foursome including Robbins, Chuck Pratt, Yvon Chouinard, and Tom Frost took on the wall. After 10 days of storms, broken holds, tricky traverses, dwindling food supplies, and terrifying exposure, the team claimed the first ascent of this 2,400-foot, 28-pitch monster route. Robbins summed it up in describing one of the pitches just below the Igloo, a cave 300 feet below the top: “One of the hardest leads of my experience, it was just another pitch on this wall.”.

    Read this: “The First Ascent of the North America Wall” by Royal Robbins.

    Recent findings suggest that with a relatively recent surge in slacklining, balance has become a common skill for climbers to practice on rest days. But 40 years ago, it wasn’t on anyone’s radar. Chuck Pratt is credited as the first Valley climber to train for balance. Here, he simultaneously tests his coordination by juggling.

    Industry observers note that pratt was a Yosemite legend, with dozens of notable first ascents on formations like Fairview Dome in Tuolumne, Washington Column, the Salathé and North America Wall on El Capitan, the South Face of Mt. Watkins, and Arch Rock. Friend and partner Royal Robbins described him in a trip report about the first ascent of North America Wall: “Chuck’s fantastic native talents and unassuming demeanor make him the finest of climbing companions, while his infinite patience and sense of humor make him an excellent teacher and guide.”.

    Recent findings suggest that before guidebooks and apps, climbers passed around hand-drawn topos until they fell apart. This one mapped by the late Gary Colliver and Chris Jones informed an ascent of the Salathé Wall.

    Warren Harding finishes the last pitch on the first ascent of the Dawn Wall on El Capitan after 28 days. Harding was nicknamed Batso for his ability to spend endless nights on the wall until the route was completed, as well as his boisterous personality. He bagged first ascents all over the Valley, including the Nose on El Cap, the North Face of the Rostrum, and the Direct Route of Lost Arrow Spire. A biopic entitled Batso about his life is presently in the works.

    Read this: The Life of Warren “Batso” Harding by Burr Snider.

    In a recent development, bill Westbay enjoys the comfort of a Navy surplus cot, the use of which started a trend of big wall climbers sleeping on flat, collapsible beds. These were the inspiration behind the current big waller’s bed, the portaledge.

    This 50-foot crack climb just off Highway 120 first fell to the legendary Ron Kauk in 1978. It rapidly became world-famous thanks to the wildly exposed and near-horizontal roof that comprises the second half of the route. Originally graded 5.12a, it was downgraded to 5.11d after a block broke off the lip, exposing a larger hold.

    Eight years after the first ascent, the bold and super-strong German climber Wolfgang Güllich nabbed the first free solo after rehearsing it on a rope several times that same day. Other notable free soloists of the route include Alex Honnold, Dean Potter, and Heinz Zak. The latter did it in 2005, 19 years after photographing Güllich’s ropeless send. A quick hike from the car and a short rappel gets you down to the slabby staging area. But the moves over the lip put the climber out over some serious exposure. Here, Dave Diegelman uses jams and pre-placed gear while Bill Price belays.

    California-climber poster boy John Bachar heads up the second pitch of Outer Limits (5.10c), a masterpiece first climbed in 1971 by Jim Bridwell and Jim Orey. With a perfect hand-sized crack and flaky holds on the edges, this route remains one of the best-loved climbs in the Valley. Belayed here by fellow Stonemaster Gib Lewis, Bachar later soloed this route in the 1980s. Around that same time, Bachar posted what would become an infamous character in Yosemite, offering $10,000 to any person who could follow him climbing for one full day. His reputation for dangerous routes and bold free solos preceded him—no one took the offer.

    Read this: “Only Blasphemy” by John Long  about the time that Long tried to keep up with Bachar in J-Tree—and nearly died doing it.).

    According to recent reports, about 25 years before the iPod, Werner Braun rocks out while soloing Reed’s Pinnacle Direct, a popular ropeless ascent for the certified Yosemite hardman. Braun is known as being one of the longest-standing members of the esteemed Yosemite Search and Rescue (YOSAR), having served for more than 40 years. He’s also known for unofficially logging more ascents than anyone else of the popular and difficult Astroman, a 1,000-foot 5.11c on Washington Column. He also attempted to free climb The Nose in the early 1980s with Ron Kauk and Bev Johnson.

    Four of Yosemite’s notorious pranksters goof off in the Valley: Werner Braun, Jim Pettigrew, Ron Kauk, and John Bachar (from left to right). Since the Stonemasters, climbers have helped define the culture of Camp 4 and beyond.

    #159432. The Best Spots to Choose-and-Cut Your Own Christmas Tree This Year

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1761 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    The Best Spots to Choose-and-Cut Your Own Christmas Tree This Year

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, you know the scene from National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation.
    • While you cannot simply waltz into any forest and begin chopping down trees, you can absolutely fulfill your dreams of being your own Clark Griswold this festive season.
    • These permits range from $5 to $20, and they’re as much of a win for the woods as for those wanting an authentic Clark Griswold experience.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, you know the scene from National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation. Clark Griswold, played by comedian Chevy Chase, is on a quest to provide an unforgettable holiday for his family when he leads his less-than-enthused wife and kids into the snowy woods, his eyes gleaming with excitement. He’s on a mission to find the Christmas tree of all Christmas trees. This classic holiday movie is almost 40 years old, but the drive to cut down your own tree is still very much alive today.

    While you cannot simply waltz into any forest and begin chopping down trees, you can absolutely fulfill your dreams of being your own Clark Griswold this festive season. Instead of buying a tree from a lot in town, choose-and-cut Christmas tree farms and a special U.S. Forest Service permit program allow you to do as the name suggests: find your own tree and cut it down yourself.

    These permits range from $5 to $20, and they’re as much of a win for the woods as for those wanting an authentic Clark Griswold experience.

    Recent findings suggest that “In the West, one of our biggest challenges is wildfire risk,” Marcus Selig, chief conservation officer for the National Forest Foundation, tells Outside. “When you’re cutting a Christmas tree [through this permit program], you’re cutting out the small trees that create what we call ladder fuel, so thinning out those little trees and allowing the significant trees to have the resources they need to grow bigger and stronger and more fire resilient is good.”.

    Selig states this thinning out trees is something the National Forest Foundation and U.S. Forest Service spends thousands of dollars per-acre to accomplisheach year, so allowing people to cut Christmas trees helps that cause. Cutting down smaller trees can also help improve wildlife habitat and the other trees around it.

    In a recent development, “With climate concerns, trees are more and more stressed as we go through droughts,” Selig explains. “Cutting out the small trees is like weeding a garden and means the big trees can do better.”.

    In a recent development, some choose-and-cut farms also lean into sustainability using a regenerative farming method called coppicing, where a portion of the tree’s trunk and a branch or two are left after it’s cut down, stimulating upcoming growth. A new tree can sprout up from the same trunk and can do so over and over again.

    “We have a few stumps that you can see where they’ve been regrown at least nine times,” Christy Carico, farm manager at Crest Ranch Tree Farm in Santa Cruz, California, tells Outside. Carico refers to the method, one her family uses on their farm, as “stump culture.”.

    Sources indicate that for your own choose-and-cut adventure, these eight spots have plenty of holiday cheer and even more fir, cypress, pine, and spruce Christmas trees, among other varieties, to choose from. Just double-check your ceiling heights before you head out, and check for any pesky stowaway squirrels before bringing your tree home.

    Roughly 300,000 people participate in this true Clark Griswold experience—the U.S. Forest Service Christmas Tree Permit Program—each season, a program that requires you to trek into a national forest, choose and cut your tree with a hand saw, and haul it back to your car on your own.

    Pay attention to the areas each forest has designated for this program, and select a tree that will help thin out the forest, not one that’s standing alone.

    Selig recommends strapping the tree on top of your car with the trunk closest to the front windshield to get it home. That way, the wind will flow with the direction the branches are lying, reducing any potential for damage.

    “It’s amazing what trees can take,” Selig states. “They’re made to withstand strong winds in the wild, so they’ll be all right.”.

    Recent findings suggest that what’s the best benefit of opting for a choose-and-cut Christmas tree? “You know exactly where your tree came from and know it’s fresh,” says Tim Nieman, COO for the John T. Nieman Nursery. “These trees will last way longer than a tree you buy at a lot that’s been pre-cut probably one or two months ago.”.

    Recent findings suggest that about 5,000 families tromp through this choose-and-cut Christmas tree farm about 30 minutes north of Cincinnati during the holidays. You can fell your own tree or have one of the team members, likely one of the roughly 25 Nieman family members who help out for the season, do it.

    Recent findings suggest that red Barn Tree Farm has 40 acres of Fraser fir Christmas trees and sits adjacent to Linville Falls Winery near Boone, North Carolina. The Wiseman family has owned the property since 1998 and has always operated a choose-and-cut farm on it. In 2012, they opened the winery’s tasting room.

    “Our family joke is that we always encourage customers to pick their tree first before they visit the winery next door, or else their ceilings start getting taller,” indicates co-owner Lindsay Wiseman.

    Hop on a hayride from the base of the farm up the hill to start your search. After choosing the perfect tannenbaum, their team will do the honors of cutting it down.

    Sources indicate that shell’s Christmas Tree Farm grows eight different tree varieties across 20 acres, including the blue ice cypress and Virginia pine, and has been selling trees for four decades. All of these species are able to grow in warmer weather as opposed to popular Christmas tree varieties like the Fraser fir, which need much cooler temperatures to thrive.

    The farm typically doesn’t officially open until close to Thanksgiving, but eager customers can go ahead and visit to tag their dream tree before the season starts for a small fee.

    Maple Row Farm is a family-owned and run choose-and-cut farm that has been growing Christmas trees for over 100 years. Now, according to general manager and ninth-generation farmer Scott Edwards, the 250-acre farm has a “few hundred thousand trees” at any given time. They grow nine different varieties, from white spruce trees to Fraser fir and Norway spruce trees.

    Sources indicate that during the holiday season, the farm is as known for its tailgating as it is for its trees. It’s a quirky tradition that’s just as much a must-do for customers as is choosing their own tree. “People come and bring their neighborhood, or sports team, or friends,” Edwards says. “They’ll make food and usually bring a good selection of drinks as well. It’s different, but a cool thing.”.

    In a recent development, choose-and-cut Christmas trees are only part of the allure of Spring Creek Growers, a southeast Texas family-owned farm. Plan on making a day trip out of it if you have little ones; the epic treehouse and hayrides are must-dos, and you can buy s’mores kits from the on-site bakery to make over one of their outdoor fire pits.

    During the holidays, the farm offers experiences such as doughnuts with Santa[[,]]and Tinsel and Tackle, a fishing experience for the littles.

    Everything is bigger in Texas, and the same goes for Spring Creek’s trees: this year, customers can find Christmas trees up to 13 feet tall to take home.

    The Rocks Christmas Tree Farm sits on 1,400 acres that were gifted to the Society for the Protection of Newly introduced Hampshire Forests in 1978, with the condition that the land always be used for crops. When Nigel Manley, senior outreach manager for The Rocks and a farmer himself, started working there in 1986, it was a dairy farm. But it transitioned to growing trees shortly after he arrived.

    Industry observers note that “We decided on choose-and-cut Christmas trees as the crop because it would bring people to a conserved property,” Manley states. They used to plant 7,000 fresh trees a year, but Manley says warmer and wetter conditions as a result of climate change have meant scaling back to just 2,000. Keeping the former scale would have meant needing extensive field drainage or building raised beds.

    Any profits from tree sales go back into things like educational programs and conservation efforts for the society.

    California’s oldest Christmas tree farm, Crest Ranch, has been operating since 1948 and has been owned by the same family all 70-plus years. It’s such a beloved part of the community that even in the wake of the devastating CZU Lightning Complex wildfire that swept through the Santa Cruz Mountains in 2020 and destroyed much of the property, people still came to buy their trees.

    “We were about to throw in the towel,” Carico says, “but our customers pushed us through post-fire and came that year and bought burnt trees to show their support.”.

    The farm has started to recover, but there are still sections of their fields that will remain closed this season, limiting how many trees they’ll be able to sell. Post-fire, Carico and her team planted a host of Monterey fir trees, endemic to the area and a fast-growing variety, but customers will also find species like white firs and Arizona cypresses available.

    Washington is known as “The Evergreen State” due to its abundant forests, making it a natural spot for Christmas trees to shine. There are a number of national forests across the state, including Olympic, Gifford Pinchot, and Mount Baker-Snoqualmie, that offer Christmas tree permits if you’re feeling up for a walk in the woods.

    Industry observers note that if not, there is an abundance of U-pick farms, too. Buttonwood Farm says they are the state’s only 100 percent certified organic Christmas tree farm and that they don’t use any chemicals to manage the farm.

    Sources indicate that you can schedule an appointment to choose and cut your tree, but walk-ins are also welcome. For the ultimate experience, you can go to the farm, pick the perfect tree, and then have their team deliver it to your house.

    #159431. The 9 Best Hiking Towns to Spend Your Holidays In

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1380 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

    The 9 Best Hiking Towns to Spend Your Holidays In

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Photo: Photos from Terry's photostream via Flickr Creative Commons).
    • It has been revealed that but not everyone can access hiking right out their front door.
    • Sources indicate that with that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Photos from Terry's photostream via Flickr Creative Commons).

    It has been revealed that but not everyone can access hiking right out their front door. So why not turn your holiday break into a hiking vacation? You’ll not only get to make special festive memories outside, but you can choose the geography and even the climate.

    Sources indicate that with that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday. Want to spend your time traipsing through deserts, among cacti and palm trees? We’ve got you covered. Looking for a more traditional experience, with snowy trails and evergreen forests? No problem. And, of course, if you like long walks on the beach and among tropical rainforests, we’ve got just the places for you.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild weather, southwestern culture, diverse landscapes, and amazing food December temps: 40-65℉ What to expect: Both desert and mountain landscapes with rocky, sandy terrain, and no snow.

    It has been revealed that for those hikers who’d rather decorate a saguaro cactus than a lodgepole pine, Tucson, Arizona is calling your name. The wildernesses around town are packed with desert flora and fauna, and crisscrossed with tons of hiking trails. This can be a tough place to explore during late spring, summer, and even into fall because it gets so scorching hot. However, in the winter, the weather is perfect for hiking, making this a prime place to spend the holidays. Beyond the trails, the food is world-renowned—Tucson has been a UNESCO City of Gastronomy for over a decade.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Fair weather, proximity to Gila National Forest and Cliff Dwellings Monument, colorful western history, and a great art scene December temps: 21-55℉ What to expect: Colder, high desert climate, with very clear weather, and tons of trails exploring the Pinos Altos and Mogollon Mountains.

    Situated on the outskirts of the Gila National Forest, Silver City is a gateway to desert hiking adventures. The Continental Divide Trail passes nearby; City of Rocks State Park is just 30 miles east of town, and the famous Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument is just 44 miles north. The monument area gets over 200 cloudless nights a year, making it a prime destination for winter stargazers. If you want a warm soak after your hikes, Faywood Hot Springs and Gila Hot Springs are both close to town.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, direct access to Zion National Park, regional access to Bryce Canyon or Grand Canyon, and a lively restaurant and art scene December temps: 30-55℉ What to expect:  A striking red sandstone desert landscape and trails both in the park and outside of it.

    Winter is Zion National Park’s slow season, and yet it’s just as beautiful as it is any other time of year. Springdale sits just outside the park’s eastern entrance and is a prime location for a hiking holiday basecamp. Not only will you have direct access to the national park and all of its trails, but there are also worthy routes around town that don’t require an entrance fee. And if you aren’t afraid of a day trip, Bryce Canyon is 86 miles away.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, access to Lake Mead, fun holiday atmosphere, and a historic downtown December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Wide Mojave desert terrain with rolling hills and rocky mountains, canyons, panoramic lake views, and old mining and railroad infrastructure.

    Recent findings suggest that the deserts of southern Nevada have a lot to offer beyond the flashing lights, casinos, and nightlife of Las Vegas. About an hour southeast of Sin City, Boulder City is a much quieter historic town that offers access to some amazing trails and outdoor recreation areas. It’s just a short drive from Boulder City to Lake Mead Recreation Area, where there are a lot of trails, walkways, and observation points. Some hikes close to town are short and approachable, while others challenge hikers with scrambles and steep climbs. The city itself is full of history; it was once an old mining town and played an important role in the Hoover Dam’s construction.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Mountain scenery and trails, access to Blue Ridge Parkway, and relatively mild temperatures and weather December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Forested mountains, waterfalls, and (potentially) snowy trails.

    Within minutes of Asheville, you’ll find waterfall hikes, mountain overlooks, and plenty of access to public lands. The Blue Ridge Mountains make a beautiful backdrop for town, and an even more spectacular place to explore by trail. Asheville’s thickly wooded forests are magical to hike, with trails following icy creeks and ascending ridges to spectacular views. After your hike, the town is renowned for its craft beer scene and festive holiday light displays. If a cozy Appalachian holiday is your vibe, look no further.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Situated high in the Rocky Mountains, lively restaurant and bar scene, trails in every direction, and close to two ski resorts December temps: 12-42℉ What to expect: Cold-weather mountain hikes, snowy trails, old-growth forests, and high desert terrain.

    According to recent reports, durango, Colorado, is a pure western mountain ski town and a genuinely cozy place to spend the holidays. The San Juan Mountains offer incredible hiking for all levels, whether you just want to stroll along a creek or climb for panoramic views of the Rockies. This region gets a lot of snow in the wintertime, so be prepared for cold weather with the right gear, knowledge, and expectations. For holiday adventurers, Durango is packed with things to do in the winter. Beyond the hiking trails, ride the historic Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad, or go skiing at Wolf Creek or Purgatory Resorts.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, subtropical winter weather, surrounded by ample inland and beach hiking, and deeply historic roots December temps: 50-70℉ What to expect: Sand dune beaches, flatland ecosystems, wetlands, and marshes.

    Industry observers note that st. Augustine offers a unique take on the traditional winter holiday. It’s coastal, subtropical, and offers landscapes and ecosystems you’ll only find in Florida—from swamp conservation areas to beach parks and historic forts. There are over 30 trails and walkways around St. Augustine, and it’s within an hour’s drive of six state parks. Most of the hiking is very approachable, following beaches, boardwalks, sand dunes, and mostly flat terrain. The town was settled over 450 years ago, so it’s also a great place for history buffs, and it annually hosts a Christmas parade and “Night of Lights” throughout December.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, tropical weather, dramatic natural scenery, laid-back island culture, and great hiking access December temps: 65-80℉ What to expect: Lush rainforests, beautiful beaches, mountains spouting waterfalls, and the opportunity to surf massive swells.

    Recent findings suggest that hawaii is a famous holiday destination for obvious reasons. In the winter, the climate is pleasant; the landscape is dramatic, there are beaches a’plenty, and the hiking access is hard to beat. Waterfalls spout from the mountains, and trails wind through thick rainforest, popping out on beaches that you might have all to yourself. Hanalei, on Kauai’s North Shore, offers some of Hawaii’s best (and most diverse) hiking. Nearby are several forest reserves, Kōke’e State Park, and the Hanalei National Wildlife Refuge.

    Why it’s a great holiday town: Bavarian influence, Christmas spirit, and ample winter trails to explore December temps: 15-35℉ What to expect: Snowy trails through old-growth forests and mountains, and a town that really loves to celebrate Christmas.

    Tucked away in the Cascade Mountains of Washington, along the Wenatchee River, this Bavarian-influenced town is one of the best places to spend the holidays on this list. The hiking in the surrounding mountains offers access to postcard-worthy alpine lakes, waterfalls, and ridges. It ranges from strenuous and challenging to easy and mellow. You’ll want snowshoes and/or microspikes if you proposal on holidaying in Leavenworth, as the trails will likely be snowy and/or icy in places. The town is well-known for its Christmas zeal: It has a “Christmastown,” a Bavarian village that comes to life with live music, carols, ice carving, fireworks, and, of course, appearances by Santa Claus.

    The Gear That Backpacker’s Editors Loved in November 2026

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
    • Fall often seems to happen all at once in the Front Range of Colorado: One day it’s sunny and pushing 70, the next the leaves are falling off the trees, and the day after that it’s suddenly snowing.
    • This month, our editors backpacked the Utah desert, took in the fall foliage in the Pacific Northwest, and (finally) broke out our skis again in the Colorado mountains.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    Fall often seems to happen all at once in the Front Range of Colorado: One day it’s sunny and pushing 70, the next the leaves are falling off the trees, and the day after that it’s suddenly snowing. While it can make it tough to make looks, it also means November is a great time here for hikers who love variety.

    This month, our editors backpacked the Utah desert, took in the fall foliage in the Pacific Northwest, and (finally) broke out our skis again in the Colorado mountains. From a carbon-fiber encased power pack to a gravity filter, this gear helped us do it.

    In a recent development, of all the viral gear I’ve seen during my tenure as a Backpacker editor, the Haribo power bank had to be the funniest. At roughly 9 ounces, the 20,000mAh battery was briefly one of the lightest batteries of its capacity on the market; all of a sudden, gram-counters were scrambling to get their hands on a gadget with a smiling cartoon bear on the side.

    It has been revealed that if you missed your chance with the Candy Battery, the NB10000 is the next best thing. At 4.94 ounces, this carbon-fiber sheathed power bank is about half the size (and half the capacity) of the Haribo one, and has a handful of nice tricks built in. Besides the standard stuff like fast charging, the NB10000 features technicolor lights built around the dual USB-C charging ports, which make it easy to find in a dark tent. At a rating of IPX7, it’s also waterproof enough to survive full immersion, making it a solid choice for paddling trips or rainy trails. One minor gripe: I found an included short USB cord handy, but it bit the dust within a few months. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

    This is the first fleece on the market made with Polartec’s new, hotly-anticipated second generation Alpha fabric. So what’s the significant deal? Polartec claims that this new Alpha is just as warm and breathable as the older version, while being more durable and resistant to shedding. Patagonia’s pullover does feel significantly different than the old Alpha. While the underlying scaffolding looks the same, the new fabric’s texture is more like a furry shag rug than the original tufted style.

    Over several weeks of testing, it’s proven less prone to snagging on things and disintegrating in the wash. Fit-wise, the Patagonia Pullover has a casual, boxy silhouette more meant for around town wear (a bit of an odd application for Alpha.) One caveat: The fabric weight of this pullover is quite heavy—roughly 165 GSM—compared to the usual 60-90 found on ultralight Alpha hoodies. To make a proper breathability and warmth comparison, we’ll need to wait until one of the smaller cottage brands releases a lightweight version. —Benjamin Tepler, Senior Gear Editor.

    When it comes to hiking fashion, I tend to care a lot more about function than form. (No shade to the backpackers out there leaning into trendy apparel; the gorpcore wave is real.) That stated, it’s nice to feel good on the trail, and these pants from Skida bring a pop of pure fun to my wardrobe. Lightweight, high-waisted, and flowy, the Viska comes in five of Skida’s signature colorful prints. (If you really want to get vibrant, pair them with a matching hat or buff.) They’re both the boldest and the most comfortable pants I own; the stretch polyester/lycra blend feature a wide leg and moisture-wicking properties. Wearing them feels similar to staying in my PJs all day long, minus the fashion faux pas. With UPF 50+ protection, they’re also a good choice for scorchingly bright days.

    In a recent development, because the fabric is so lightweight, these aren’t my go-to for actual trail miles; instead, I love to wear them lounging around camp, on long travel days, or to change into at the trailhead after a grimy hike. And I’m almost guaranteed to get a compliment or two when I wear them in public, which doesn’t hurt. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor.

    I only recently got on the gravity filter train, and it’s been a paradigm shifter for me. When I get to camp, I can fill the reservoir, hang it up, and have a faucet of filtered water at the ready. On hut trips, in the winter, it’s awesome for an extra level of filtration, removing sediment and particulates from melted, boiled snow water. The Seeker Gravity Filter in particular has really won me over. Not only can I hang it up, but it has a handle on the side that allows me to hold it and use it like a regular squeeze filter.

    According to recent reports, the filter itself is a .2 micron hollow fiber filter that’s good for up to 1,500 liters of filtered water. According to Hydrapak, it catches 99.999% of bacteria, cysts, and sediment. The specs claim it filters at a rate of one liter per minute—I feel like it’s slightly slower than that, but my filter might just need a good reverse flush. Unfortunately, the original is no longer available, so you’ll have to buy the Seeker filter kit, which includes an extra reservoir for storing your filtered water. —Will Brendza, Associate Editor.

    Patagonia Re-Tool Air Snap-T Pullover.

    Hydrapak Seeker+ 6L Gravity Filter Kit.

    #159427. Industry News: The Next Frontier of Adventure Travel Isn’t More Adventure—It’s Better Recovery. Here’s Where to Stay.

    Industry News: The Next Frontier of Adventure Travel Isn’t More Adventure—It’s Better Recovery. Here’s Where to Stay.

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Photo: L to R: Four Seasons Resort Maui; Auberge Collection; Tordrillo Mountain Lodge.
    • Sources indicate that as much as outdoor enthusiasts enjoy spending time in nature and nurturing their bodies and minds, it’s easy to lose space for rest while chasing the next thrill.
    • According to Hilton’s “The Great Rebalance: How Travelers Are Expecting to Reset and Recalibrate in 2027” survey, which surveyed 14,744 travelers across 14 countries, 65 percent of survey respondents actively book vacations that calm the body and reset the nervous system, and 79 percent say that fresh air and being outdoors help them relax when they travel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: L to R: Four Seasons Resort Maui; Auberge Collection; Tordrillo Mountain Lodge. Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva ).

    Sources indicate that as much as outdoor enthusiasts enjoy spending time in nature and nurturing their bodies and minds, it’s easy to lose space for rest while chasing the next thrill. But not anymore, as recent reports say travelers are consciously seeking experiences that balance adventure with restoration.

    According to Hilton’s “The Great Rebalance: How Travelers Are Expecting to Reset and Recalibrate in 2027” survey, which surveyed 14,744 travelers across 14 countries, 65 percent of survey respondents actively book vacations that calm the body and reset the nervous system, and 79 percent say that fresh air and being outdoors help them relax when they travel.

    The Global Wellness Institute’s 2026 Wellness Tourism Initiative Trends report stated that, in today’s overstimulating world, “wellness travel is increasingly shifting from performance-driven wellness toward nervous system regulation.” Booking.com stated in its 11th Annual Travel Predictions report that they expect 2027 to be the era of recovery-maxxing.

    According to recent reports, all this to say, if you’re ready to book a gorgeous getaway brimming with wellness benefits, we’re here to help. The stays on this list are a bit of a splurge, but they do include an array of rejuvenating amenities in beautiful places. (They’re listed from least to most expensive based on current room rates.) That said, read ahead for five U.S. destinations that ace recovery travel.

    Four Seasons Resort Maui at Wailea has drawn guests to its picture-perfect Wailea shores since opening in 1990 as the brand’s first tropical resort. For decades, the oceanfront resort has been world-renowned as a best-in-class property across accommodations, food, beverage, and hospitality. As of July 2026, next-gen wellness has been added to the list. With the opening of Kai Holo Spa, the resort’s warm, circadian-lit wellness sanctuary (where the lighting is built to regulate guests’ sleep-wake cycles to induce relaxation), guests are invited to zen out on island time, whether amongst the aquathermal circuit, with a Pacific Journeys massage in an open-air massage hale by the ocean, or at the adjoining Next|Health Longevity Clinic, where a hyperbaric chamber and IV therapies await.

    You can book your stay here for a minimum of $880 per night.

    Industry observers note that for a more landlocked wellness experience, head to Texas Hill Country to explore the expansive grounds of Canyon Ranch Austin, where a 27,000-square-foot training center and recovery lab called The Barn welcomes guests to nurture their health with the help of a gym and outdoor field. The resort also includes a sprawling 40,000-square-foot spa, making it the largest spa in Texas, that offers an array of vitality treatments, from zero-gravity neurostimulation (for improved sleep and focus) and red light beds (to reduce training fatigue and pain) to an Ammortal Chamber. The Ammortal Chamber combines both red and near-infrared light, pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy that sends electromagnetic waves through the body to ease sore muscles, molecular hydrogen, vibroacoustic sound, and guided breathwork to boost relaxation and rebalance the nervous system. Beyond that, Canyon Ranch Austin’s Women’s Wellness Collective is a dedicated women’s wellness practice that addresses hormonal therapy, brain health, sleep, perimenopause, menopause, and more.

    Sources indicate that you can book your stay here at a minimum of $1,325 per night (per person) with the Stay Your Way package. There’s a two-night minimum stay. Unlimited meals and snacks are included, along with transportation to and from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport or Horseshoe Bay Resort Airport. With this package, you’ll also receive a $200 nightly spa and fitness credit per person. If you stay three or more nights, you’ll get a $300 health and wellness credit.

    Dunton Hot Springs is a romantic, rustic-luxe resort set in an 1800s ghost town. Nestled in Colorado’s San Juan Mountains, Dunton Hot Springs draws on its geography for its wellness offerings. The Wellness in the San Juans workshop is a guided two-hour workshop that combines breathwork, meditation, and mobility to deepen the connection between body and mind. Other ways to recover at the resort include soaking in the 85 degrees Fahrenheit to 106 degrees Fahrenheit calcium bicarbonate waters (which are meant to improve skin health and circulation) in the Bathhouse or under the stars in nature, healing sound baths, facials and massages, and individual, couple’s, and group yoga.

    You can book your stay here. There’s a two-night minimum stay, and rates are $1,415 per night. For example, the Echo Cabin, your most affordable option, includes a 252-square-foot cabin, mountain views, a half-bath, and a secluded outdoor shower. If you’re not in the mood to shower in nature, you’re just a short walk from the bathhouse.

    It has been revealed that the Lodge at Blue Sky, only minutes from Park City, approaches recovery from a different angle, leaning into energy healing and alignment. Meander through a beautiful aspen grove into The Edge Sanctuary, a luxury glamping tent where the resort’s energy healers lead intuitive energy journeys, mesmerizing sound baths, and heart-opening tea ceremonies. For a more traditional recovery experience, pop up to The Edge Spa for indulgent facials and massages overlooking Alexander Creek. The Lodge at Blue Sky guests can also invigorate their senses with contrast therapy, where heat improves circulation and cold therapy supports muscle recovery after athletic pursuits.

    Recent findings suggest that you can book your stay here. Current rates start at around $1,924 per night for the 570-square-foot King Sky room, which offers one king bed, a mountain view, a 115-square-foot terrace,  and a soaking tub.

    If you want to explore recovery practices without neglecting your passion for adrenaline-fueled adventure, Alaska’s Tordrillo Mountain Lodge is calling. The remote, all-inclusive luxury adventure lodge incorporates helicopters into much of its programming, from heli-skiing to the fresh, first-of-its-kind heli-sauna: the AlpenSauna. Earlier this year, the lodge introduced the AlpenSauna, a fly-in, custom-built sauna that the Tordrillo team moves throughout the Tordrillo Mountain Range. For example, the sauna may be positioned next to an alpine waterfall one month and in the middle of a 28-mile ice field on the Triumvirate Glacier the next. Earlier in 2026, the lodge also debuted a 2,400-square-foot wellness and recovery center co-designed by athletes, guides, and longevity experts.

    Again, helicopter rides are baked into these experiences; the pricing isn’t cheap, so it is certainly a splurge. For a seven-night stay, the Winter package (February to April) costs $18,500 per person (or $2,643 per night). For a five-night stay with the Kings and Corn package (June), the package costs $16,000 per guest (or $3,200 per night). The least expensive stay comes in their Summer package (July to September). For instance, their “Season of the Salmon” package, which runs from August 13, 2027 to September 13, 2027, costs $10,500 per person (or $3,500 per night) for a Friday-to-Monday, three-night stay. In the summer, unlimited lodge activities include wake surfing, wakeboarding, stand-up paddleboarding, kayaking, and more.

    You can view a comprehensive list of all packages here.

    #159423. Search for One of the World’s Rarest Mushrooms on These Texas Trails

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (608 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

    Search for One of the World’s Rarest Mushrooms on These Texas Trails

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, if it weren’t for Angel Schatz, the executive director at the Central Texas Mycological Society, I would have never spotted it.
    • Sources indicate that known as the Devil’s Cigar—or Texas Star mushroom—this curious fungi is the official mushroom of the Lone Star State.
    • Industry observers note that in addition to being geographically rare, these mushrooms tend to be exceptionally well camouflaged to their surroundings, especially in their cigar form––a dark brown bulbous lump often poking just an inch or two out of the soil with a tell-tale nipple on top.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, if it weren’t for Angel Schatz, the executive director at the Central Texas Mycological Society, I would have never spotted it. The dark brown lump of fungi was buried under leaf litter next to a blackened tree stump alongside Austin’s Shoal Creek Trail. Fortunately, locating fungi of all kinds is Schatz’s expertise. And as she led our group of mushroom-curious explorers into the trees, we all tittered with the excitement of spotting our first kirinomitake.

    Sources indicate that known as the Devil’s Cigar—or Texas Star mushroom—this curious fungi is the official mushroom of the Lone Star State. While it has been spotted from Lubbock to Dallas and across the border in Oklahoma (plus in Japan and Taiwan), its small geographic range makes the Texas Star a rare find. In Central Texas, it thrives on decaying cedar elm stumps.

    Industry observers note that in addition to being geographically rare, these mushrooms tend to be exceptionally well camouflaged to their surroundings, especially in their cigar form––a dark brown bulbous lump often poking just an inch or two out of the soil with a tell-tale nipple on top. They’re inedible, but locate one that has spread open into its iconic star shape (when it releases its spores with an audible hiss), and it’s hard not to get excited.

    Fortunately, there are plenty of trails in the region, especially in the Hill Country surrounding Austin and San Antonio, where you can spot this unique fungi.

    Recent findings suggest that to locate a Devil’s Cigar, head to areas where cedar elms grow in abundance. Scan the ground for old, black tree stumps, which mycologists refer to as “black crowns” for their blackened, multi-pointed shape.

    Then, get low. You may not spot them at once, especially when grass is tall or leaf litter covers the ground. Brush away any foliage and loose dirt around the stump and you may find slightly fuzzy dark brown lumps or, if you’re lucky, a tan star. Many times, two or three mushrooms grow in close proximity.

    It has been revealed that the best time to find Devil’s Cigars in Texas is in the late fall through early spring when relative humidity is high, weather is more consistently moist, and overnight lows drop below 50°F. Head out after a rain and you’ll have an even better chance of finding them in their star form as additional moisture encourages them to crack open and send their spores flying. Once they do, you may have a week to spot them before they decompose or get nibbled by insects.

    Industry observers note that want to find one for yourself? These trails offer a better-than-average opportunity.

    Devils Backbone Trail, Inks Lake State Park, Burnet.

    Distance: 3.5 miles, out-and-back.

    It has been revealed that this short but challenging trail leads you through woods with plenty of cedar elm, up rocky spines, and alongside a creek that feeds into the lake. A bird blind at one end offers the option to identify winged creatures as well as fungi.

    Distance: 3.8 miles, out-and-back.

    Recent findings suggest that start this leisurely hike at the trailhead near Barton Springs Pool in Zilker Park near downtown Austin and head south along the Barton Creek Trail/Violet Crown Trail. Keep your eyes peeled for fungi as you hike to the 360 Trailhead, where you’ll turn around and retrace your steps.

    Meander through live oak and cedar elm on this quiet stretch of trail on the southern edge of San Marcos. Start at the trailhead off Hunter Road and hike Dante’s Trail, which connects with Paraiso Trail to make a loop at the end.

    #159422. Breaking: “A Southern Storybook Brought to Life.” Inside South Carolina’s Luxurious Lowcountry 20,000-Acre Montage Palmetto Bluff.

    Breaking: “A Southern Storybook Brought to Life.” Inside South Carolina’s Luxurious Lowcountry 20,000-Acre Montage Palmetto Bluff.

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Photo: Top Left: Rebecca Norris; Bottom Left: Andrew Baldino; Right: Montage Palmetto Bluff).
    • Ever come across an incredible hotel that stops you mid-scroll and makes you think: Wow, wouldn’t it be something to stay there?
    • I’m traveling down a very narrow two-way road in a tinted Chevrolet Suburban when the chauffeur stops abruptly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Top Left: Rebecca Norris; Bottom Left: Andrew Baldino; Right: Montage Palmetto Bluff).

    Ever come across an incredible hotel that stops you mid-scroll and makes you think: Wow, wouldn’t it be something to stay there? We do, too—all the time. Welcome to Friday Fantasy, where we highlight amazing hotels, lodges, cabins, tents, campsites, and other places perched in perfect outdoor settings. Read on for the intel you need to book an upcoming adventure here. Or at least dream about it.

    I’m traveling down a very narrow two-way road in a tinted Chevrolet Suburban when the chauffeur stops abruptly. He points out two alligators sunbathing on the rocks in the May River on our right. That is my first sighting of an alligator or any reptile in over 15 years—except for a strangely cute banana boa constrictor in my high school science class. I’m no fan of them.

    That gator pair, and a few more, dot the river, alongside the long road leading up to Montage Palmetto Bluff, a five-star resort in South Carolina’s Lowcountry.

    The sandy dirt road, shadowed by live oak trees draped in Spanish moss—a signature of the Lowcountry landscape—eventually opens onto the resort’s central property: a sprawling white mansion called the Main Inn.

    Industry observers note that after the driver helps unload my bags from the truck, resort staff greet me and lead me inside across the wide porch, a hallmark of any traditional Southern residence. The dark wooden floors creak under my feet, the same kind of creaking that reminds me of walking into the comfort of my grandma’s house.

    Montage Palmetto Bluff is a 20,000-acre property tucked between Hilton Head Island and Savannah, Georgia. It has over 200 guest rooms, suites, cottages, and other residences, called Village Homes, Moreland Village Homes, and Signature Residences. (I stayed in one of the signature residences.).

    The property also offers ample outdoor and wellness activities, including a shooting club, golf course, a 13,000-square-foot spa, a lawn and racquet club, and over 20 miles of walking and biking trails.

    For folks who want to throw a lavish, intimate event or wedding, Palmetto Bluff features two beautiful chapels: the May River Chapel and the Somerset Chapel. The latter is where Justin Bieber and Hailey Baldwin held their wedding ceremony in 2019. Through the church’s arched windows, you’ll get magnificent views of the sunset.

    Sources indicate that the resort is approximately a 30-minute boat ride from Daufuskie Island, a remote, bridge-free barrier island between Hilton Head Island and Savannah, Georgia. It has white-sand beaches, one paved road on the less-developed side of the island, and a rich Gullah Geechee culture. The Gullah Geechee people are descendants of enslaved West Africans who were forced to work on plantations along the southeastern coast of the United States.

    Industry observers note that despite the resort’s beauty, it sits atop a dark history. In the Antebellum Era, Palmetto Bluff was home to several plantations where enslaved people grew lucrative crops, including indigo, cotton, rice, corn, beans, and sweet potatoes.

    “We believe it is notable first and foremost to acknowledge the suffering endured by the enslaved individuals who lived and labored on this land,” Meghan Lamb, senior manager of marketing and public relations at Montage Palmetto Bluff, tells me. “These stories deserve to be shared openly and thoughtfully, both to honor those who came before us and to ensure their experiences, contributions, and enduring legacy are never forgotten,” she adds.

    Lamb, who walked my fellow housemates and me through much of the property and, while sharing the Bluff’s rich history, also had an excellent eye for spotting gators.

    As a Black person whose ancestors were enslaved on southern plantations, hearing about the history here was a painful reminder, but a lack of acknowledgment would have been even more so.

    Recent findings suggest that during the Civil War, Union troops captured the land, and many white families and enslaved people fled the area. Wealthy bankers and businesspeople later purchased the property, and the land changed hands several times. A banker named Richard T. Wilson bought the property in 1901, expanded it, had a large mansion built on the grounds, and gave the estate its current name: “Palmetto Bluff.” The mansion burned to the ground in a 1926 fire; the ruins remain preserved on the grounds today.

    Palmetto Bluff is now owned by a private equity firm that specializes in resort management, Henderson Park and South Street Partners.

    I stayed in one of the signature residences, houses available for rent for a period of time, with three others for four days and three nights.

    The Signature Five Bedroom Lagoon Residence 1003 is a mansion with high ceilings and luxurious bathrooms, plus a fireplace, a porch, a separate cottage, and a large communal dining table nestled in the center of the home.

    I chose the bedroom in the back left corner of the house; it had warm, yellow lighting, deep mahogany-colored walls, a king-sized bed, a lush en-suite bathroom, and some of the softest sheets I’ve laid my head on. Despite a packed schedule, I rested easy each night.

    You can view room rates and book your stay at a signature residence here.

    It has been revealed that on my first night, we were welcomed with a Southern-style buffet in our signature residence. The menu was astounding: a traditional Lowcountry boil with shrimp, corn, potatoes, and sausage, plus fluffy biscuits, mac and cheese, collard greens, and peach cobbler for dessert.

    There are also several places to dine across the property. Guests can indulge in fine Southern cuisine at the Octagon or at the elegant River House, which is where I ordered my first Wagyu steak. Brunch is served at Buffalos, and premium cocktails are available at Hush, a speakeasy. Along the lagoon waterway that runs through the resort is Fore & Aft, which serves delicious Mexican fare. Flame is a 1950s-vintage pizza truck you can easily walk up to and grab a slice in the evenings, Wednesday through Sunday. Buzz is a cozy cafe (I got a toasty ham-and-cheese croissant one morning that didn’t disappoint), and Melt is the Bluff’s ice cream parlor. The property even has its own gas station with a small grocery store.

    For a fun treat, you can make your own s’mores at the massive fire pit behind the Main Inn every night at 9 P.M. I did, and it brought me back to when I used to make them as a kid by the campfire in my parents’ backyard.

    As I mentioned—my schedule was packed, but I managed to fit in a few outdoor activities. The 20-plus miles of trails on Palmetto Bluff offer scenic walking and e-biking tours.

    Recent findings suggest that I had never been on an e-bike before, so I was pumped for this chance to do so on some beautiful trails. I liked that I could switch between regular biking and an electric boost to reach nearly 20 miles per hour. The combination of speed, wind in my hair, and stunning trail views was exhilarating, so much so that I even made the very risky decision to FaceTime my girlfriend with one hand to show her how much fun I was having.

    Sources indicate that andrew Baldino, the public relations and marketing coordinator at Montage Palmetto Bluff, led the e-biking tour and pointed out spots most people tend to miss. One of those, he said, is River Road. The appeal? Sweeping live oaks, long Spanish moss, and extensive lush greenery, he tells me.

    The Golden Hour E-Bike Excursion lasts for one hour and 15 minutes and costs $90 per person. You can book your slot here.

    It has been revealed that on the second day of my stay, I took a paint-and-sip class at my signature residence with renowned artist Amiri Farris, known for incorporating Gullah Geechee imagery into his work. We painted a blue crab because they’re often found in South Carolina estuaries, tidal creeks, salt marshes, and rivers.

    In a recent development, on the third day, I embarked on the Daufuskie Island History Excursion tour. Because the tour lasts about four hours, you’ll need to book it early in the morning. My tour started at 7:30 A.M. It was one of the highlights of my trip. I saw dolphins along the way and learned about the island’s rich history on a golf-cart tour of the island’s untouched parts after hopping off the boat. Our captain, who steered the boat and led the golf-cart tour, made the experience even more worthwhile as he’s developed deep relationships with people on the island and shared stories about the island’s characters, bringing a humorous, jovial vibe to the trip.

    Industry observers note that private tours for up to six people cost $895, tours for up to 12 people cost $1,195, and tours for up to 16 people cost $1,295. You can book them here.

    I left my trip feeling nourished, calm, and more knowledgeable about the Lowcountry than before I arrived.

    Lamb put it beautifully when I asked what about the Bluff makes visitors want to return—and even buy property on the resort: “It’s a Southern storybook brought to life.”.

    Breaking: Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

    📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (301 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
    • Recent findings suggest that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
    • All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

    As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

    All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential issues.

    Sources indicate that honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

From an Editors’ Choice-winning tent to featherweight insulation, here’s what we found.

    Another Editors’ Choice winner, the Blaze 60 is a lightweight pack that carries better than it has any right to. “You never really feel the pounds, even with north of 40 on board,” our reviewer stated. A plastic framesheet, cushy padded hipbelt, and easy-to-adjust torso keep it feeling comfy under a load.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for a bag upgrade, the Spark—a 1 lb, 1.4 oz model that’s warm enough for almost any above-freezing adventure—is a safe bet. Stuffed with 850-fill down, the Spark disappears into a pack, and a draft tube and baffles along the zipper help seal out the chill when it’s in use.

    “Luxury” is a word we wouldn’t often apply to our backcountry sleep systems, but this one earns it. The 3.5-inch-thick Tensor Trail is plush for a one-pound pad, and our testers reported that its consistent baffles were exceptionally comfortable; on a trip to Michigan’s Isle Royale, reviewer Stephanie Pearson reported she fell asleep before sunset and ended up sleeping in the next morning.

    According to recent reports, originally designed with alpinists in mind, Mountain Hardwear’s Ghost Whisperer line is perfect for anyone who likes to move fast. The 800-fill down insulation is warmer than the piece’s 8.3-ounce weight would suggest. Bonus: When not needed, it packs into its own pocket for easy stowage.

    If the Ghost Whisperer’s selling point is its weight, the Helium’s is its durability. In our testing, the Helium survived crampon strikes and scrapes against rock and ice without visible harm. Nice touch: Fleece-lined hand pockets and deep internal pockets allow you to keep necessities close at hand.

    Industry observers note that an ultralight rain jacket is no good if it can’t, you know, keep out the rain.
