    • With lift ticket prices regularly topping $250 across North American mountains, budget skiing takes strategy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    This year, beat high lift ticket prices by volunteering as a patroller, adaptive ski instructor, or buy qualifying flight tickets to a number of select locations (Photo: South_agency/Getty Images).

    With lift ticket prices regularly topping $250 across North American mountains, budget skiing takes strategy. Outside dug into this season’s best hacks for scoring free lift tickets for skiers and snowboarders, from airline promotions at nine marquee resorts, to volunteer opportunities, and even to going downhill with a U.S. Forest Service ranger.

    This winter, we’re tracking the snowiest mountains in America and the rare super El Niño on the way. Now, here’s what you need to know for the 2026-27 winter season when it comes to snagging your free passes.

    Industry observers note that located in the San Juan Mountains of Southwest Colorado, Purgatory Resort is a 30-minute drive from Durango. With over 1,600 acres and an average snowfall of 260 inches annually, the mountain offers a blend of steep tree skiing and open groomers.

    During the 2026-27 season, Purgatory is offering skiers and snowboarders a free season pass in exchange for 14 days of volunteering. Four of those shifts must fall during peak season, including winter holidays, Presidents’ Day weekend, and spring break.

    Recent findings suggest that several other mountains across the country offer similar incentives for those volunteering on the slopes. Winter Park Resort in Colorado, North Carolina’s Beech Mountain Resort, and Whiteface in Upcoming York all provide free lift tickets in exchange for volunteering on ski patrol or the safety team.

    In a recent development, alaska Airlines’ Atmos Rewards Alpine Getaways for the winter ski season lets passengers show a qualifying boarding pass at nine participating western U.S. and Canadian ski resorts for free lift tickets, rental upgrades, and resort discounts.

    Eligible passengers flying into the following airports get a free full, same-day, or half-day ticket.

    Jay Peak Resort in Vermont is celebrating its annual Day for the Devoted on November 27, 2026, featuring 750 free lift tickets.

    Industry observers note that “Day for the Devoted opens the season with a thank you to the people who make this place what it is, and an invitation to anyone ready to become a part of it,” the resort writes on its website. You can register for the event here.

    Buying a qualifying Helly Hansen ski jacket or pair of pants gets you a free day or a buy-one-get-one ticket at participating resorts across North America and Europe. Clothing must be from the latest Helly Hansen ski collection.

    Buy your gear, find the resort you’d like to ski, and submit your receipt to redeem a pass. More information is available on the company website here.

    Industry observers note that adaptive skiing nonprofits rely on volunteers to help people with disabilities experience skiing. In many cases, volunteers receive a complimentary lift ticket for the day they’re helping.

    It has been revealed that at Eagle Mountain Therapeutic Recreation in Showdown, Montana, volunteers 16 and older can receive free passes and lunches on the days they work. Those who work four events can receive a day pass to be used at any time, while those who commit to eight or more days will receive a free pass for the season, according to the program website.

    Recent findings suggest that the Outdoors for All at The Summit at Snoqualmie and Stevens Pass in Washington offers a variety of volunteer programs, from ski and snowboard instructors to support in snowshoeing and Nordic skiing. Full-time volunteers are eligible for a discounted season pass, while part-time volunteers receive a same-day lift ticket. All volunteers also receive ExpertVoice pro deals and have access to instructor development, adaptive teaching experience, and clinics.

    Every Friday beginning January 30 through April 3, 2027, intermediate skiers and snowboarders can spend an hour skiing with a U.S. Forest Service (USFS) staff member through the Ski With a Ranger Tour. Attendance is first-come, first-served and limited to 12 participants daily.

    Industry observers note that participants must provide their own lift ticket, but the program is part of a free conservation education initiative that shares the USFS mission in ski area management. Participants will also learn about natural resources and environmental stewardship, the USFS writes on its website.

    Sources indicate that kelso Carapia, a recreation specialist with the USFS Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit, has been leading the program for 14 years. She told Outside that participants can expect to learn about a host of topics, including water ecology, forest health, animals, survival strategies, fire management, general land stewardship, and the cultural and geological history of the Tahoe Basin.

    According to recent reports, ski experience is necessary. The route is on intermediate and blue terrain only, and skiers will access at least two lifts as part of their tour.

    “This is not a ski lesson,” Carapia noted. “It is an interpretive tour. As much as we prioritize safety and comfort of our participants, we are not there to instruct.”.

    Heavenly Mountain Resort straddles the California-Nevada border in South Lake Tahoe, California, and Stateline, Nevada. With 4,800 skiable acres across four base areas, it’s also a major winter destination.

    Ski With A Ranger tours are led by the United States Department of Agriculture’s Forest Service Conservation Education staff and volunteers through a cooperative effort between the Forest Service and Heavenly Mountain Resort.

    #159417. 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1637 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tinybeans ↗ Open Full Page

    21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement.
    • Even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being.
    • The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more important to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

    Even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less key than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy indicates. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”.

    The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

    When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

    1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

    According to recent reports, 2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

    3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

    It has been revealed that 4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up states, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

    It has been revealed that 5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

    6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

    7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

    Sources indicate that 8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

    For parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he says. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

    9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

    10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

    In a recent development, 11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

    Recent findings suggest that 12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

    Recent findings suggest that 13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

    14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

    Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

    In a recent development, 15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

    Sources indicate that 16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a newly introduced way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

    According to recent reports, 17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

    According to recent reports, 18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

    Sources indicate that for activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

    19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

    20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

    21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!

    It’s that time again. Yup, your Elf on the Shelf is about to parachute in to make your life (slightly) more challenging for the next few weeks. Get ahead of the game and prep your bag of tricks with these brilliant ideas. From Elf on the Shelf clothes to last-minute Elf on the Shelf ideas that’ll make the whole family giggle, we’ve got enough easy Elf ideas to last you the entire holiday season.

    According to recent reports, I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves. Not going to lie, remembering to move the thing every night was a struggle. But when I made the effort and managed to pull off even the easiest of Elf ideas, the look in their eyes was priceless.

    1. Elf held captive. If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun. Pull out a toy train and a string, and decide which elf is going to be extra naughty by tying up the other one.

    According to recent reports, 2. Plan a hot cocoa party. This is fun on the first night or maybe on a weekend day. Get mugs, instant cocoa, and marshmallows set up in advance and settle the elves against the mugs. Snag printables for the party here.

    3. Spell it out. Do you have Scrabble tiles or Bananagrams? Then it’s a cinch to let your elf leave a sweet message for your littles to discover the next day.

    Recent findings suggest that 4. Caught in the act. With this easy elf idea, you’ll use a bag of M&Ms, chocolate chips, or even a box of sugar cereal, and position your elf with its backside out of the bag.

    5. Exhausted elf. All those trips up to the North Pole make for one tired elf. Let your little one in red take a day off. Make them a little bed with a doll blanket and a cotton ball for a pillow.

    6. Deeds worth doing. Since reporting good deeds to Santa is your elf’s duty, it’s the perfect opportunity to remind kids about the spirit of Christmas. We dig the free downloadable from Over the Big Moon.

    7. Elf spaghetti. Whip up Buddy the Elf’s favorite dish for your little helper. Hint: this is a great idea for the night you make pasta. You’ll also need syrup (of course), marshmallows, candy, and chocolate syrup. Find out how to make a batch over at Instructables.

    8. Riding the banister. Those naughty elves are always looking for an adrenaline rush! Use a Frisbee and sticky tape to get your little buddy set up at the top and ready to ride.

    In a recent development, 9. Sitting pretty. Have your elf take a seat inside your wreath or on the holiday table for a picture-perfect spot.

    10. Play games. Set up your elf mid-move with this adorable mini-Twister printable.

    According to recent reports, 11. Window view. If you’ve got a window and a curtain rod, you’ve got a sweet spot to hang your elf. Easy-peasy.

    Sources indicate that 12. Rock climbing wall. All you need is several pre-made bows to make a route for your elf.

    13. Coloring elf. Take 30 seconds to scribble in a coloring book or on a printable, scatter crayons, and set up your elf. Giggles are guaranteed!

    15. Zipline. This Elf on the Shelf idea is popular, but it does take a little time to set up. All you need is string or yarn, a candy cane, and a way to secure your elf to the candy cane!

    Recent findings suggest that 16. LEGO throne. Whether you use DUPLO or LEGO, making a seat for Santa’s little helper can be done in less than five minutes.

    In a recent development, 17. Elf in the kitchen. Got a play kitchen? Then let your elf whip up something yummy.

    18. On the road. With a toy car, your elf can go just about anywhere they want to go. Headed to buy a Christmas tree? Done. Want to take Wonder Woman out on a date? Totally!

    Recent findings suggest that 19. Play Picasso. A dry-erase marker, a family photo, and a sense of humor are all you need. Give your kids beards and cat ears: See how much they laugh!

    It has been revealed that 20. Put the elf in the freezer. Your elf sure does miss the North Pole! Give him a little time to chill.

    21. Toilet paper tricks. Add an elf to a roll of toilet paper and send them down the stairs. Don’t have a second level? Leave a trail of written messages down the hall instead.

    22. Bath time. You don’t need a Barbie bath to let your Elf soak aching bones— a plastic bowl or storage container will do the trick. Add marshmallows for bubbles, and you’re set.

    23. Gone fishing. Your kids will love waking up to find the elf “fishing” for goldfish crackers in the bathroom sink.

    24. Story time. Position the elf with a favorite holiday book and a captivated audience.

    According to recent reports, 25. Hanging by a limb. Any elf will feel right at home when dangling from a branch of the Christmas tree.

    26. Spa day. Wrap your elf in a paper towel, give them cucumber eye patches, and just like that, it’s a spa day.

    In a recent development, 27. Puzzle play. Settling your elf in for the night with a puzzle is easy and fun.

    Industry observers note that 28. Paper bag race. Take those lunch bags that have been cluttering your drawer and collect a few stuffies. Then, stage a sack race-style scene across your dining room table or kitchen island.

    According to recent reports, 29. Elfie selfie. Position your elf in front of the family laptop and snap a picture. Just be forewarned, if it’s a laptop you use, you’ll need to get it set back up before the kids get home from school.

    30. Sweet snow angels. It’s not quite as cold down here as it is at the North Pole. When your elf gets antsy for chilly weather, make them a personal snow angel. You can use flour (but it’s messy), sprinkles, or rice, which is my personal favorite because it’s the easiest to clean up!

    31. All wrapped up. Give your elf the scissors, tape, and wrapping paper. Scatter shredded paper and tape around, and it’ll be like they were caught in the act of wrapping up Santa’s gifts!

    According to recent reports, 32. Elf making popcorn. Someone’s ready for family movie night!

    Sources indicate that 33. Don’t move the elf. Well, it looks like your kids were so well-behaved that no North Pole reporting was needed. It’s also the perfect excuse for one of those nights you forget to move them.

    It has been revealed that 34. Cards, anyone? Didn’t you know elves love to play games? They do, and they love to be caught mid-game.

    35. A Stuck Elf. This is a super-easy elf idea, and you don’t even need the message board to pull it off. Just grab a mason jar or an empty water bottle and a prominent place to display your elf’s tight situation.

    36. S’more to love. Some toothpicks, roasted marshmallows, chocolate squares, graham crackers, and tea lights are all you need to set up this cozy and easy elf idea.

    37. Read all about it. Prop them up on a favorite Christmas story or beloved book.

    It has been revealed that 38. Caught red-handed. Have your elf stage a scene of questionable actions and tape up the area with crepe paper.

    39. Photo editor. They can’t help but make mischief, and marking up a festive photo is a silly way to say, “Elf wuz here.”.

    Recent findings suggest that 40. Riding dinos. If you’ve got a plastic dinosaur (T. rex preferred), then you’ve got what you need to give your elf a prehistoric ride.

    41. Send the Elf back to the North Pole. Possibly one of our favorite easy elf ideas: on Christmas Morning, make sure they’re out of sight, and of course, leave a note.

    The Best Way to Avoid a Meltdown When iPad Time Is Over

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (272 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them.
    • Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta recently shared her method for successfully ending iPad time, and it combines a little bit of the two approaches above with some voice modulation and sensory input.
    • In a recent development, A few things to note about this method.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them. Whether you resort to a countdown timer or go the “this is your last show” route, it’s pretty much always a struggle.

    Perhaps you need a new strategy. Parenting coach Dr. Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta recently shared her method for successfully ending iPad time, and it combines a little bit of the two approaches above with some voice modulation and sensory input.

    In a recent development, A few things to note about this method. Using language like “We have one more song” instead of “This is our last song before we leave for school” focuses on what the child is doing now versus what you are doing in the future. It’s easier for kids to accept the transition this way.

    “Melodic intonation” is when you use a sing-songy voice to make a statement. It helps kids notice what you are saying and acknowledge it. Take a look at Miss Rachel and a lot of the other preschool-focused programming, and you’ll see it employed often. Using melodic intonation for the phrase “iPad is all done” helps to signal the transition for the child.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s important to remember that even when using a technique like this, it will take you doing it the same way over and over several times before your child catches on and gets with the program. If they have a meltdown, don’t engage; stay calm; and move on.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, as grandparents, you want all of your relatives to feel happy, loved and connected in your manufacturer. Unfortunately, that doesn’t always happen.

    Sometimes, unintentional or even well-meaning comments from grandma and grandpa can “create an environment where grandkids feel uncomfortable or insecure,” Ann-Louise Lockhart, a pediatric psychologist and president of A Latest Day Pediatric Psychology in San Antonio, told HuffPost.

    That’s why it’s notable to be more mindful about how we communicate with our grandkids not just during this time but all year round.

    “It can be hard to change the way you say things but it’s important to be intentional with your words, and be aware of how much words can impact the way your grandkids think and feel about themselves and their relationship with you,” Lockhart said.

    We asked Lockhart and other experts which common phrases are best avoided and what to say instead.

    One note before we dive in though: If you’ve used any of the below phrases before — or happen to slip up in the future — try not to worry too much or beat yourself up over it.

    “It’s never too late to start being more mindful of how you approach interactions with your grandchildren,” stated Andrea Dorn, a psychotherapist and author of the “Mindful Steps” children’s book series.

    “It undercuts parental authority, which can have long-standing consequences,” she said. “Furthermore, it models for kids that they might find themselves in situations where it’s in their ‘best interest’ not to tell their parents. This can be especially dangerous if a child is being groomed by a predator or feels bad about themselves for getting bullied.”.

    Instead, you want to reinforce the importance of being honest with their parents — no matter what.

    “Grandparents can find other ways of doting on their grandchildren without crossing the boundaries their parents have put in place,” Delawalla noted.

    Comments about a child’s body or weight are a “huge no,” Lockhart said, as they can contribute to body image and self-esteem problems.

    According to recent reports, “As responsible adults, it’s our duty to support and encourage children to be confident in their own skin,” she said. “Let’s avoid making any comments that could potentially harm their self-worth and lead to insecurity. I hear about it constantly in my practice from young children through adults. Harsh comments from grandparents like this are remembered and replayed over and over again.”.

    Industry observers note that dorn also told HuffPost that any remarks or comparisons about physical appearance can be problematic. This includes things like: “Have you lost weight?” or “Wow, you’re so much taller than your brother now!”.

    “The glitch with comments about physical appearance or comparisons to others is that they place an increased focus on the importance of external features over internal traits,” she said.

    Instead, she suggested saying something like: “It’s wonderful to see you again! I’ve missed spending time with you. How have you been?” Open-ended questions about your grandkids’ current interests, activities or hobbies are great, too.

    “Being genuinely interested in who kids are on the inside helps them to feel seen and heard, and sends the message that each person can be valued just as they are right now and that people are more than just how they look or what they wear,” Dorn said.

    Any comments about your grandkids’ food intake — “You eat so fast,” “You’re a member of the clean plate club,” “Looks like you haven’t touched a thing on your plate” — are best kept to yourself.

    Industry observers note that “Learning about food and hunger cues is an crucial developmental step in childhood,” Dorn said. “Comments about ‘good’ and ‘bad’ eating habits can influence children to adjust their eating behavior in reaction to another person’s comments or perspective, rather than following the signals their body is sending them. It may also trigger feelings of shame or confusion in the moment or over time.”.

    It’s really not necessary to comment on your grandkid’s plate or their eating habits. But if you’re going to say something, Dorn recommended focusing on the importance of listening to one’s body.

    Sources indicate that “You can also model this practice by listening to your own body, and stopping when you feel full and eating when you feel hungry,” she said. “Modeling good eating habits is more important than any comments we can make.”.

    When you see your grandchild acting ungratefully while opening a mountain of presents or throwing a fit because they didn’t get their way, you might be inclined to make a comment about how spoiled they are.

    If this kind of behavior is happening pretty consistently, it probably has less to do with the kid and more to do with the way they’ve been parented.

    Sources indicate that as Ryan Howes, a clinical psychologist from Pasadena, California, told HuffPost: “If they are acting entitled and ungrateful, this may be a behavior they learned or saw modeled for them, maybe even something that was reinforced by their parents. So giving them all the blame isn’t fair. Suck it up or talk with the parents, but keep the judgment to yourself.”.

    It has been revealed that as a grandparent, it’s natural to want to connect with your grandchildren in this way, especially when you’re so excited to see them. However, many kids may not feel comfortable giving hugs and kisses on demand, and it’s crucial for the adults in their lives to respect this.

    “While this phrase is likely filled with love and a completely normal desire to foster closeness and connection with a child, it can also unintentionally take away a child’s right to autonomy and pressure them to abandon and second-guess their body boundaries,” Dorn said. “This can send confusing messages about consent.”.

    In a recent development, in order to respect your grandkids’ boundaries, you could instead phrase this as a question: “I’d love to give you a hug. Is that OK?”.

    But if they say “no,” accept their answer and move on.

    “Make sure not to push further or use guilt with a comment like, ‘Please, just one? I’m your grandma/grandpa!’” Dorn said. “A helpful thing to do instead is keep the mood light and say something like, ‘OK! I love you so much and can’t wait to hear all about what you’ve been up to.’”.

    It’s never too late to start being more mindful of how you approach interactions with your grandchildren.

    You can also suggest other ways to connect like waving hello or goodbye, or giving a fist bump or a high five.

    In a recent development, “Kids often feel like they don’t have a lot of self-determination, so it can be a powerful message to send that vital grown-ups in their life will respect their body boundaries no matter what,” Dorn mentioned. “This approach also reinforces the idea that physical affection is a personal choice, promoting a healthy understanding of boundaries and consent in other areas of their life.”.

    Parenting styles and best practices change over time. You may have raised your children in a different way than your adult children are now raising their own kids.

    Industry observers note that “Of course, grandparents grew up in a different era with different customs and norms, and it’s natural to want to comment on the differences,” Howes mentioned. “There’s nothing inherently wrong with pointing out these distinctions, but it’s very easy for those comments to come across as shaming. By shaming, I mean declaring that one way was right and another is wrong, and that there is something wrong with the grandchild or their parents.”.

    Generally speaking, it’s best to keep those comments to yourself unless you see “significant blindspots or areas that could potentially be harmful for the child,” Howes remarked. “Even then, it’s best to take concerns to the parents instead of the grandchild.”.

    Sharing these kinds of judgments or negative comments about your adult child’s parenting choices with your grandkids is not a good idea, he said.

    “If grandparents have a beef with how their child is parenting, they should bring it up to them or keep it to themselves, but leave the grandchildren out of it,” Howes said.

    The original version of this story was published on HuffPost at an earlier date.

    If you don’t give a toddler something to do, they’ll find their own source of entertainment—and that can be a terrifying prospect (you know the feeling if you’ve suddenly noticed the house is too quiet only to find that they’ve somehow given themselves bangs). To keep them out of trouble and thoroughly entertained, we’ve rounded up some awesome games for toddlers that are sure to be a hit, whether you’re indoors or outdoors. The best part? Your kiddo won’t know it, but they offer ample opportunities for hands-on learning. Ready for endless fun? On your mark. Get set. Go find your tot’s latest fave!

    Sources indicate that toddlers are bundles of energy: always on the move, always growing, always learning. Learning with play is essential for their development because it improves small and large motor skills, muscle strength, emotional intelligence, language development, spatial awareness, and more. According to an article by Michael Yogman, MD, FAAP, on Healthychildren.org, “research reveals play can improve children’s abilities to plan, organize, get along with others, and regulate emotions. In addition, play helps with language, math, and social skills, and even helps children cope with stress.”.

    Figuring out how to keep toddlers engaged is no easy feat. There are outdoor games, indoor games, toys, beginner board games… You get the idea. The key is to decide which activity is right for your kiddo, and that depends on factors like their age, energy level, developmental stage, and other milestones.

    One of the most important things to consider is what interests your toddler. Do they love Ms. Rachel? Are they obsessed with a sport? Do they love baby dolls or animals? Once you figure out what will keep them interested, you can go from there.

    Another factor is something called Play Schemas, a concept first used by Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget. As stated in My Play Cupboard, Play Schemas are repeated patterns of behaviour you notice children engaging in when they play. Nine schemas can be commonly observed in young children, including connection, transforming, enveloping, enclosing, and positioning.

    Once you figure out which Play Schema your toddler is drawn to, that will help you decide what type of games they’ll enjoy the most.

    Give your jumping bean something to jump about—letters! We love that this outdoor game from The Imagination Tree combines alphabet awareness with the chance to get those wiggles out. Simply write letters in sidewalk chalk and have your little one hop from one to another as you call them out. And all you need to get started is a set of sidewalk chalk. Read all about it and check out the phonics and math variations over at The Imagination Tree.

    Recent findings suggest that let your toddler be your boss with a few rounds of Simon Says. Toddlers love the chance to be in charge! Then, you can give the commands for a bit. It's silly, active, and engaging—that's why it's an early childhood classic. Plus, it gives little ones a chance to practice following instructions, taking turns, and building listening skills. Simon Says go play!

    Industry observers note that toddlers love climbing under, over, and on top of all sorts of things. Obstacle courses let you take that natural climbing instinct and make it a game. Build an indoor obstacle course with painters' tape, making lines for your little one to walk on top of and jump over. Or take the fun outside and challenge them to stay off the grass in the yard or the wood chips at the playground. Ready for a bonus round? Turn the obstacle course game into follow-the-leader and take turns being the leader. Check out this post for even more obstacle course fun.

    In a recent development, kids of all ages love a good scavenger hunt. Send your toddler on a hunt through the house for four red things or two things with wheels. If you have a little more time or an older toddler ready for a challenge, print out a scavenger hunt like these. Good news: they're all free!

    We love the Easy Boat Activity from Toddler Approved because it's budget-friendly, and it uses supplies you've already got in the house, like plastic containers, tape, and straws. Kids love it because it offers indoor water fun and the chance to capsize a fleet of tiny ships. Sail down to Toddler Approved to find out how you can set up your own version. Don't miss Kristina's ideas about what to talk about with your little one as you play to turn this game into a toddler-friendly science experiment.

    Whether it's Five Little Monkeys or Ram Sam Sam, toddlers dig a good tune. Plus, rhymes and songs like these are more than just fun. They build toddlers' vocabulary and pre-literacy skills. Find upcoming ones to add to your repertoire at Storyblocks, a site created by Colorado librarians to share rhymes and songs for toddlers and preschoolers.

    Industry observers note that toddlers go gaga over games that give them a chance to put stuff in a container and then dump it out, so this Oatmeal Container Straw Game from Merriment Designs is bound to be a hit. We love that this game made out of recycled materials packs a major dose of fun on a budget. Round up straws and an empty oats container, then head over to Merriment Designs to find out how to make your own.

    If your toddler is anything like ours, Mama Papa Bubba's DIY Felt Board is bound to be a massive hit because it's all about ice cream. Felt ice cream, that is. Little ones can practice fine motor skills and learn about colors as they match each colorful scoop and dot. Plus, when you've had your fill of ice cream, the board makes a perfect background for felt animals or people that can be used for storytelling fun. The possibilities are endless! Find the step-by-step instructions to create your own felt board at Mama Puppa Bubba.

    In a recent development, stretch it out and play a game of animal yoga with your little one. You can pick up a set of soft yoga blocks that toddlers can toss up in the air before diving into a downward-facing dog. Or try out these five animal yoga poses and pretend to be stretching tigers and rolling bears.

    eeBoo's Life on Earth has everything we look for in a memory game: sturdy pieces, beautiful eye-catching images, and the chance for game-playing fun. If your kiddo isn't quite ready to play a full game, pull out a smaller set of matching cards for mini-memory fun. Plus, talking about the pictures on the cards is a guaranteed vocabulary builder.

    Available at amazon.com, $21.99.

    Recent findings suggest that try the dress-up challenge: give your toddler a scenario or career, like summertime, rainy day, forest animal friends, sports star, or construction worker, and send them off to create an outfit that meets that challenge. They can use their own clothes or dig things out of the dress-up bin. Then, put on a tune that goes along with the scenario you've picked and put on a fashion show. We guarantee that you'll get lots of fantastic photos out of this game! It's also great to play after dinner to encourage little ones to put on their PJs. Last challenge: bedtime!

    According to recent reports, most board games are still a little tricky for young toddlers—but Where's Bear from Peaceable Kingdom is just right. Little ones get to play hide-and-seek with little bear, stack the sturdy cardboard blocks, and learn new words as they play.

    Available at amazon.com, $24.95.

    In a recent development, even if it's raining cats and dogs, your toddler can play Melissa and Doug's bowling game for hours. The weighted bottoms on the six soft animal pins make them easy to stand up, and the set comes with a carrying case for on-the-go fun and storage. Kiddos will build their gross motor skills and can also practice counting the pins one by one. Strike!

    Available at amazon.com, $32.99.

    In a recent development, caught waiting in line or at a restaurant without a stocked bag of goodies? Then pull out the animal guessing game, a game we love because it requires no gear. Think of an animal and ask questions until your game playing buddy guesses it. Does it have legs? Does it live in a tree? Older twos and three-year-olds love this game. When you're playing with younger toddlers, change it to the animal sounds game: make a sound (MOOO!) and have the toddler guess what kind of animal makes that noise. Then switch it up and have them make the sound.

    Industry observers note that your toddler will spend lots of time spelling their name and piecing together words with this Magnetic Rainbow Busy Box from Mama.Papa.Bubba. It can be an art project just to create the box and they'll have endless fun learning and spelling once it's finished.

    What are the benefits of toddler games?

    Playing games with your toddler is not only a great opportunity to enjoy quality time with your child, but they help develop key life skills like problem solving, small and large motor skills, physical coordination, hand-eye coordination, and learning how to be social with others.

    What types of games are best for toddlers?

    While it depends on your child’s age, interests, and development, the best toddler games are simple and fun. Popular ideas include pretend play, memory games, music games, and basic movements, like a simplified version of Simon Says.

    How much screen time is appropriate for toddlers?

    According to the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, toddlers should have very limited daily screen time.

    According to recent reports, there are online toddler games that are designed specifically for young children. Parents should always review the game or content before allowing their child to watch, monitor usage, and opt for an ad-free, child-friendly tablet or platform.

    What are some fun indoor games for toddlers?

    Toddler indoor games should be fun and easy to set up: memory, obstacle courses, block building challenges, sensory stations, and pretend play like “the floor is lava,” “vet clinic,” and “grocery store.”.

    #159411. Why You Should Fight the Urge to Make a Happy Kid Happier

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (830 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tinybeans ↗ Open Full Page

    Why You Should Fight the Urge to Make a Happy Kid Happier

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We are walking between two tractors in a barn when I say something very stupid to my 22-month-old son.
    • And then I decide to say, “Do you think the cat is in here today?”.
    • It has been revealed that last time we were here in the fall, there was a big, gray cat who got just close enough so that my toddler could bend down, reach out the tips of his fingers, and briefly graze its arched back.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We are walking between two tractors in a barn when I say something very stupid to my 22-month-old son. We’ve been at this farm for about an hour, the kind of place where you can reach your fingers through the fence to pet the goats and stare into the pigpen and marvel at how much bigger pigs are than you think. It’s a mysteriously warm winter day, and my son has thrown his jacket off, his stroller discarded somewhere around the sheep pen. For the first time in months, we are feeling the sun on our faces. He’s having the time of his life. He’s already pet a one-day-old lamb and has discovered that in the barn we are at the moment walking through there’s not one, not two, but three tractors.

    And then I decide to say, “Do you think the cat is in here today?”.

    It has been revealed that last time we were here in the fall, there was a big, gray cat who got just close enough so that my toddler could bend down, reach out the tips of his fingers, and briefly graze its arched back. But that was enough. He’d brought up the cat for days, and I knew if he saw it again, he’d be so, so happy.

    Recent findings suggest that except there was one problem. The cat wasn’t here.

    Why did I have to mention the cat? It was a perfect moment; we were like an illustration from a children’s picture book. But now, there was only one thing my son wanted to do: find the cat. I’d reminded him that there was a cat. And he loves cats. Especially this cat, the famed cat that let him touch its fur for a fraction of a second. So of course, in a very cat-like fashion, the cat was nowhere to be found.

    It has been revealed that that’s when the tears began. The three tractors were no longer enough. The baby goats—garbage. The teeny tiny lambs, only minutes ago, he was thrilled to pet. Who needs them? It was only the cat now.

    “I don’t know,” I stated, hoping his outburst wasn’t calling too much attention to us from the less cat-obsessed farm visitors. “He’s probably sleeping somewhere.”.

    “WHERE CAT,” he demanded, over and over again.

    And just like that, I’d broken my own biggest rule of parenting: Never try to make a happy kid happier.

    According to recent reports, this rule came to me via my friend Joanna, who had learned it from her parents. As soon as she told me, I knew she’d identified one of my greatest weaknesses as a parent. I always want my son to be having a good time, and there’s some part of me that worries if I’m not actively trying to make his time better, it’s not as good as it could be.

    According to recent reports, as a baby, if he was enjoying gnawing on a particular teether, I’d jump in to give him another one, too. Oh, he likes the dog at this park? Let’s leave this park with one dog to find a dog park full of dogs. If he were having a perfectly nice time throwing rocks in a puddle, I’d offer to find him better rocks that would make an even bigger splash.

    Sources indicate that there’s an impulse in us as parents not just to nurture, to make sure all gaps are closed. We want to provide the complete package for our kids, to make sure all their needs are met in the best possible way. And that urge is good. It’s why we don’t abandon them in the woods when they won’t stop crying at 4 a.m. and why we keep feeding them every day even when they throw everything we offer on the floor. But it also means we can fail to notice when we aren’t needed.

    What “don’t make a happy kid happier” does is remind me that sometimes, just being happy is enough. Kids live in a world of the immediate now, where whatever they are doing is often the only thing on their minds. Yes, there might be bigger, splashier rocks to throw in the puddle, but the rocks they have in their hand suit them just fine. What I think I’m doing when I do this is helping my son, but what I’m actually doing is pointing out that what he’s doing might not be good enough. Suddenly he can see that the emperor has no clothes, and it actually becomes not good enough.

    We never did find the cat. But I paid the price for my misstep in toddler currency: a temper tantrum. He settled down eventually, and by the time we left the farm, he was happily kicking and chatting in his stroller. I thought about stopping for ice cream at the gift shop, but I decided against it this time. He was just fine.

    #159400. What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1131 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.
    • Nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot upcoming health topic du jour.
    • We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

    Nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot upcoming health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

    We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

    In a recent development, “I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” claims Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

    Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

    According to recent reports, inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

    It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

    “If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas says.

    Recent findings suggest that vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, states Melas.

    In a recent development, ignoring early signs of GI complications can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

    Sources indicate that “For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

    Recent findings suggest that probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

    According to recent reports, “I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He stated that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas says.

    Sources indicate that it’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

    In a recent development, “We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee indicates that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

    Ultimately, Melas claims she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

    “If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a big, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she says. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.

    Breaking: 3 Ways To Stop Your Kid From Being A Walking Petri Dish, Per A Pediatrician

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can’t germ-proof your kid, but a pediatrician states these three habits get you pretty close.
    • According to recent reports, most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride.
    • Recent findings suggest that “There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can’t germ-proof your kid, but a pediatrician states these three habits get you pretty close.

    According to recent reports, most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride. And conversely, the underlying anxiety of knowing it’s only a matter of time before they get sick and have to stay home. It’s a question worth asking: Is there anything we can do to prevent our kids from being a petri dish at school? I spoke with Dr. Brittany Odom, a board-certified pediatrician, mom, and trusted pediatric health educator, to see if she had any useful advice on preventing the many, many illnesses our children pick up this time of year.

    Recent findings suggest that “There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it. So, them getting sick is not a parenting fail,” Dr. Odom wants to first point out. She then highlighted three ways we can take action against these seasonal illnesses.

    A landing routine is what your kids do the moment they walk into your house after school. Kind of like stop, drop, and roll, minus the roll. Have them immediately remove any items from school, like their jackets, backpacks, and shoes.

    Then, kids should wash their hands. “That way, we are not tracking all of the germs from school throughout the house,” she explains. Furthermore, this is even more important for families with babies at home because “older siblings bringing illnesses home is one of the most common ways babies get sick.”.

    In a recent development, “Your eyes, nose, and mouth create your T-zone, and this area is where a lot of germs can enter our bodies,” shares Odom. So simply emphasizing to our children to keep their hands away from this area is majorly helpful. Furthermore, if kids are apt to touch the T-zone regardless of what you say, enforcing handwashing is obvious, but worth stating again. “Washing hands at the most key times is helpful too. So, before we eat, after we use the bathroom, and before touching a baby sibling.”.

    If we can also teach kids to cough and sneeze into their elbow instead of their hands, that’s one more way to prevent the germs from entering the T-zone.

    “Have a basket already set up with everything you need at 2 a.m. when your kid wakes up with a fever and they’re feeling terrible,” Odom recommends. These are the products Odom suggests having in there, and luckily, they are all easily shoppable in stores and online:.

    Beyond these three tips, Odom recommends that all children ages 6 months and older get both the flu and COVID vaccine. (Mom tip: An easy option for accomplishing this is CVS’s MinuteClinic, which is faster and oftentimes more convenient than a trip to the doctor’s office.).

    Sources indicate that additionally, if you have an infant under 8 months old entering their first RSV season, and you did not receive the maternal RSV vaccine during pregnancy, talk to your pediatrician about getting this one too. It's also approved for babies 8 months to 19 months old who are considered "high risk.”.

    Industry observers note that “Send your kids back when they are fever-free for at least 24 hours and symptoms have dramatically improved,” claims Odom. As much as we want them out the next day, sending them back sick is harmful and disruptive to other students. And you don’t want to be that mom!

    According to recent reports, since typical cold care medicines aren’t recommended for children under 4 years old, Odom states to focus on “supportive care.” These are ways to bring them some comfort and relief from their symptoms. Non-medicated saline sprays are useful, as well as a nasal aspirator. “There’s a lot of watchful waiting, making sure they are feeding well, still giving you wet diapers, and staying hydrated,” shares Odom. A humidifier is also helpful: “I recommend a cool-mist rather than warm-mist humidifier. It should be emptied and cleaned regularly to prevent mold or bacterial growth.”.

    According to recent reports, taking Odom’s words to heart, I tried to institute a landing routine today when my 3-year-old returned home from preschool. Sure, he mentioned “no” when I asked him to wash his hands. But then, with the promise of some lollipops, he reconsidered. Hands washed, he immediately ran to my 6-month-old in her bouncer. And yes, he went for her T-zone, but hey, at least his hands were clean. I’ll take the win!

    #159396. Tech Report: Yes, My Toddler Sleeps In Our Room. No, We Haven't Stopped Having Sex.

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1194 w)

    Tech Report: Yes, My Toddler Sleeps In Our Room. No, We Haven't Stopped Having Sex.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.
    • My 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me.
    • Sources indicate that to which I say: We manage just fine, thanks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.

    My 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me. I like cuddling him all night, and I’ve come to accept that it’s just the kind of mom I am: the clingy co-sleeping type. When he was littler, we took safe-sleep precautions with a bassinet and all that jazz, but these days, he sleeps right up next to me. Most non-co-sleeping families cringe at this. And then they immediately want to know: So how do you get intimate with your partner?

    Sources indicate that to which I say: We manage just fine, thanks. But lately, I’ve been wondering about the elephant in the room. Or, should I say, the toddler.

    My husband and I NEVER have sex in the bed with our toddler. But we do sneak into the bathroom. Or sometimes, once he’s deeply asleep, we pull out a cot on the other side of the room and get it on in the dark. I’m embarrassed even admitting that.

    I also don’t believe we’re the only parents who have ever found themselves in this predicament.

    According to recent reports, here’s the thing... our house isn’t huge. And between the 3-year-old sleeping soundly in our blacked-out bedroom and one of our much more aware older kids wandering out of their rooms, we’ve chosen the former.

    Which brings me to something else we really need to address. What about the “olden days”? Ma and Pa from Little House on the Prairie managed to have four babies while living in one-room log cabins and shanties. I guarantee they weren’t heading out to the barn or the outhouse every time they wanted to have sex, especially when bears and wolves were roaming around, and temperatures dipped below zero.

    Besides, many modern families around the world still live and sleep in shared spaces.

    Sources indicate that lately I’ve wondered if being horrified by the idea of parents having sex in the same room as a sleeping child is a cultural thing. Is it so awful if they’re still very little? At what point does “they have no idea what’s happening” turn into “Mom and Dad need to find somewhere else to do this”?

    We reached out to experts to answer all the questions you’ve probably been dying to know but have been way too embarrassed to ask.

    In a recent development, here’s the short answer: Parents don’t need to feel guilty about having sex in the same room as a newborn or young infant. An infant doesn’t have the “cognitive capacity to understand what sex is,” and they won’t remember or understand what’s going on, says Kimberly Resnick Anderson, LCSW, an AASECT-certified sex therapist.

    Recent findings suggest that anderson does add one caveat, though. Having a baby nearby is likely to make parents more reserved and overall less expressive during sex. Over time, she says, that could potentially lead to a “more permanent shift” in how they express themselves sexually.

    When does she recommend finding some privacy? Around age 1.

    Once a child develops language and becomes mobile, she says, it becomes harder to get it on, knowing the child could wake up in the middle of it.

    It has been revealed that but Samantha Ridout, M.Phil., BCBA, a child development and behavioral expert, cautions against treating any birthday as a universal cutoff. No two children develop at exactly the same rate, she claims, so there isn’t a magical age when a child suddenly becomes aware of what’s happening around them. Instead, parents should watch for their child’s growing alertness and awareness and set appropriate boundaries.

    According to recent reports, I’ve found this to be true in my own family. We moved our older two kids out of our room quicker because they were definitely more aware than our last, who just feels more “babyish.”.

    But both experts made one thing very clear: During sex, infants need to be in a separate, safe sleep space.

    Let’s go back to my Ma and Pa observation for a minute, shall we?

    The idea of children and adults having separate bedrooms is a relatively new phenomenon, indicates Macall Gordon, a researcher and sleep coach with an undergraduate degree in anthropology who studies children’s sleep through a sociohistorical lens. She says before the lightbulb was invented, family life revolved around sunrise and sunset, with families often sleeping in shared spaces.

    But with electricity, adults could suddenly stay up after children went to bed, she adds. Now, children needed a “separate space to sleep” while adults stayed up. So the nursery and the crib came along. Then, she notes, the layout of homes started to change, too, to include hallways connecting separate rooms. Before that, rooms were all connected to each other, so you had to go through one to get to another.

    To this day, however, a separate bedroom is still something of a privilege. Many families simply don’t have “extra, separate rooms,” Gordon points out, especially in big cities, where studios and lofts are common, or in cultures where extended family members may occupy additional bedrooms. “While we think of a separate room for children as the norm, it really wasn’t for most of our history,” Gordon shares.

    Tiffany Belanger, cosleeping expert and founder of Cosleepy, notes the topic tends to divide her followers into two camps: those who will have sex in the room with a kid and those who won’t. When I described my scenario to her, she responded that floor sex while young kids are still sleeping in their parents’ bed is actually pretty common among the co-sleeping families she hears from.

    You want to know if mine has woken up before.

    Industry observers note that but rarely. He’s a really deep sleeper, and it’s only happened a few times. It’s dark, and when he did wake up, he immediately called out for me in that disoriented, half-asleep way toddlers do. We stopped immediately. The cot is also on the far side of the bed, outside his line of sight. As far as I know, he never saw or heard anything.

    In a recent development, will we emotionally damage our kid if he were to catch us in the act? Unlikely, Ridout says, if parents stay calm, stop immediately, tell the child they are safe, and answer their questions in a simple, non-panicky way.

    But all of this still leaves me with the extremely practical question that got us into this mess in the first place.

    It has been revealed that parents have to get creative, flexible, and spontaneous, says Anderson. That might mean asking family or friends to babysit when you can, doing it in other rooms, or using whatever short pockets of privacy you can find.

    In a recent development, and while Belanger reassures me that my floor-sex solution isn't unheard of among co-sleeping parents, the other experts think it’s not a great option when kids become mobile and verbal. So, I suppose it might be time to retire the cot. Where to next?

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more.
    • It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks.
    • The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

    It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

    The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

    We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

    Industry observers note that most of the experts we polled noted one big shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” indicates Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

    Sources indicate that is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

    Amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

    Before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” claims Hanson.

    Recent findings suggest that jenn Lueke, New York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

    In a recent development, prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

    Recent findings suggest that another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

    As a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Aims change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

    But if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: initiative five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he claims.

    In a recent development, lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

    In a recent development, the trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

    Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

    Andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

    If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

    It has been revealed that “One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” states Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

    Sources indicate that don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a big proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

    Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

    Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

    However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

    You should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson notes.

    Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

    And while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

    If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

    In a recent development, “Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” notes Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

    Sources indicate that “A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

    But maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.

    Industry News: How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic
